en: The Noble Saṃghāṭa Sūtra.
May there be well-being! Homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
[SaSū 1] Thus have I heard: at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain together with a great saṅgha of bhikṣus,
namely twenty-two thousand bhikṣus, such as the venerable Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya.
And with the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana,
the venerable Śāradvatīputra, and the venerable Mahākāśyapa.
And with the Venerable Rāhula,
the Venerable Bakkula,
and the Venerable Bhadravāsa.
and with the venerable Bhadraśrī,
and with the venerable Nandaśrī,
and with the venerable Jāṅguli;
And with the Venerable Subhūti, and the Venerable Revata, and the Venerable Nandasena.
Together with the Venerable Ānanda,
twenty-two thousand bhikṣus headed by him, and sixty-two thousand bodhisattvas, such as the bodhisattva mahāsattva Maitreya.
and with the bodhisattva mahāsattva Sarvaśūra,
the bodhisattva mahāsattva Kumāraśrī,
and the bodhisattva mahāsattva Kumāravāsin;
and by the bodhisattva mahāsattva Kumārabhadra,
and by the bodhisattva mahāsattva named Anūna.
And with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Samantabhadra,
and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sudarśana.
and with the bodhisattva mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyarāja,
and the bodhisattva mahāsattva Vajrasena—
headed by these, there were sixty-two thousand bodhisattvas.
And there were sixty-two thousand sons of gods, such as the son of god Arjuna,
the son of god Bhadra,
and the son of god Subhadra.
And by the divine son Dharmaruci,
and by the divine son Candanagarbha,
and by the divine son Candavāsin.
And with the divine son Candana,
and the divine son Candanasena,
and so forth, led by these, there were sixty-two thousand divine sons.
And with eight thousand celestial maidens, namely: the celestial maiden Mṛdaṅginī,
the celestial maiden Prāsādavatī,
and the celestial maiden Mahātmasaṃprayuktā.
And of the divine maiden Varṣaśrī,
and of the divine maiden Padmaśrī,
and of the divine maiden Prajāpativāsinī.
And with the divine maiden Balinī,
and the divine maiden Subāhuyuktā—
thus led by these eight thousand divine maidens.
And there were eight thousand dragon kings (*nāgarāja*), namely: the dragon king Apalāla,
the dragon king Elapatra,
and the dragon king Timiṅgila.
And by the nāga king Kumbhasāra,
and by the nāga king Kumbhaśīrṣa,
and by the nāga king Sunanda.
And by the nāga king Suśākha,
and by the nāga king Gavaśīrṣa— by these eight thousand nāga kings, headed by such as these.
[SaSū 7] They all approached the great city of Rājagṛha, where Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa was located, and where the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat,
the Perfectly Awakened One, was staying. Having approached, they bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One,
circumambulated the Blessed One three times, and stood before him.

[They said this: "May the Blessed One teach the Dharma; may the Sugata teach the Dharma, hearing which we might quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and by which there might be the destruction of the karmic obscurations of all sentient beings.
And the Blessed One consented by remaining silent.

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and extending his joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows:

“O Blessed One, many tens of millions of goddesses, many tens of millions of celestial maidens, many tens of millions of bodhisattvas, and many tens of millions of śrāvakas have gathered and are seated to hear the Dharma.

Therefore, O Blessed One, it would be well if the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, were to teach such an entrance into the method of the Dharma for those who have thus assembled and are seated.”

May this lead to the long-term welfare, benefit, and happiness of both gods and humans; and through this teaching on the entrance into the method of Dharma as it has been shown, may all karmic obscurations of these elder beings be completely exhausted upon merely hearing it,
and may younger beings, applying themselves to wholesome qualities, attain excellence.
They would decline; they would not fall away from wholesome qualities.

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra: "Excellent, excellent, Sarvaśūra! It is indeed excellent, Sarvaśūra, that you consider it necessary to ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, about this matter."

"Therefore, Sarvaśūra, listen well and attend closely to what I shall say to you. "So be it, Blessed One," the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then said this to him: "Sarvaśūra, there is a discourse on the Dharma (saddharmaparyāya)..."
By which Dharma-discourse the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*) and the karmic obstructions of all sentient beings are exhausted,
and likewise other karmic obstructions go to exhaustion,
and they quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment— what, O Blessed One, is that Dharma-discourse of the True Dharma?
The Blessed One said:
"There is a Dharma discourse named *Saṃghāṭa*,
which shall now circulate in Jambudvīpa."
Whoever, O Sarvaśūra, shall hear this Dharma discourse, the Saṃghāṭa,
his five actions of immediate retribution will be completely exhausted,
and he shall become irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

[SaSū 15] What do you think, Sarvaśūra? Will that being who hears this Dharma-discourse, the *Saṃghāṭasūtra*, produce a mass of merit equal to the mass of merit produced by one who has performed honors for a single Tathāgata? Sarvaśūra, it should not be viewed in this way.
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said:
"How, moreover, O Blessed One, should it be viewed?
The Blessed One replied:

Sarvaśūra, those beings who hear this Dharma discourse, the *Saṃghāṭa*, shall produce a mass of merit equal to the mass of merit produced by having honored as many Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā. Sarvaśūra, all those who hear this *Saṃghāṭa* Dharma discourse shall become irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
And all shall behold the Tathāgata; all shall become those who have seen the Tathāgata; and all shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
They shall be invincible to Māra the Evil One,
and all those who hear this *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, O Sarvaśūra, shall attain that very same wholesome dharma.
They shall all know arising and cessation.

Then, at that time and on that occasion, all those bodhisattvas, great śrāvakas, gods, nāgas, humans, and tens of millions of apsarases who had assembled there rose from their seats and draped their upper robes over one shoulder.
Placing their right knees upon the ground and extending their joined palms toward the Blessed One, they all questioned the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, how much [merit is there] for one who has performed an act of veneration toward a single Tathāgata?"
"A mass of merit," the Blessed One said.
"Listen, son of good family."

The measure of the mass of merit of a single Buddha is as follows: it is like the drops of water in the great ocean, or the atoms in Jambudvīpa, or like all sentient beings equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā, were they all to become Bodhisattvas established on the ten stages; and the mass of merit belonging to those Bodhisattvas is far surpassed by the mass of merit of a single [Buddha].
[It is] the mass of merit of a Buddha.
And therefore, Sarvaśūra, those beings who hear this Dharma-discourse of the *Saṃghāṭa* will produce a much greater mass of merit;
it is not possible by means of calculation to reach the limit of that mass of merit.
Sarvaśūra, when at that time and on that occasion they hear these words, they will experience great enthusiasm and will produce such an immeasurable mass of merit.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, who are those beings who will be thirsty for the Dharma?
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra: "Sarvaśūra, there are these two types of beings who are thirsty for the Dharma."
"Which two?

Namely, Sarvaśūra, one who possesses a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings; and second, Sarvaśūra, one who, having heard the Dharma, proclaims it equally to all sentient beings. These two are those who thirst for the Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra asked: "Lord, what is the Dharma that, having heard it, is to be proclaimed equally to all sentient beings?"
The Blessed One said: "Sarvaśūra, one person, having heard the Dharma, dedicates it toward awakening.
And when they dedicate it toward awakening, then all sentient beings will become thirsty for the Dharma.
Sarvaśūra, the second person is he who plunges into the Mahāyāna; he is always thirsty for the Dharma."

[SaSū 21] Then those tens of millions of gods, nāgas, humans, and apsarases rose from their seats, joined their palms before the Blessed One, and said this to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, we are thirsty for the Dharma; may the Blessed One fulfill our aspirations and those of all sentient beings."

[SaSū 22] Then, at that time, the Blessed One manifested a smile. Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra rose from his seat, extended his joined palms toward where the Blessed One was, and addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, for manifesting this smile?"
[SaSū 23] Then the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra:
"Sarvaśūra, those beings who come here, they all realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening;
they all attain perfection for the sake of perfecting the range of the Tathāgatas."

The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said: “Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, by which these beings, having come here, realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment? The Blessed One said: “Excellent, excellent, Sarvaśūra!
It is well that you consider it necessary to ask the Tathāgata about this matter.”
Therefore, Sarvaśūra, listen!
Here, Sarvaśūra, the distinction of dedication (pariṇāmana) is to be seen.
Long ago, Sarvaśūra, in the past, incalculable eons ago, at that time—

At that time, a Tathāgata named Ratnaśrī appeared in the world— an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One. Furthermore, Sarvaśūra, at that time I was a young brahmin student (māṇavaka), while those who are now sentient beings...

At that time, at that moment, all those who were deer were established by me in the wisdom of a Buddha; and at that time, at that moment, I made this vow: "May all these deer who are currently tormented by suffering be reborn in my buddha-field, and may I establish them all in the wisdom of a Buddha."
"I shall establish them. And those deer, having heard those words, spoke these words: "So be it!
By that root of merit, Sarvaśūra, these beings, having come here, will realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
[SaSū 27] Then, having heard that encouragement from the Blessed One, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what will be the lifespan of those beings?
The Blessed One replied:
"The lifespan of those beings will be eighty-four thousand kalpas.
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra asked, "Blessed One, what is the measure of a kalpa?
The Blessed One said, "Listen, son of good family."
For example, Sarvaśūra, suppose a certain man were to build a city twelve yojanas in length and breadth, with a height of three yojanas.
Suppose he were to fill that city completely with sesame seeds (and that man were to live by his hair).
Then, after the passing of a hundred years, that man [would take] a single sesame seed from that city which is filled with sesame seeds.

By this method, that man might exhaust and completely finish all those sesame seeds by casting them outside; yet that city would remain without root or foundation, and even now the eon would not have come to an end.
Furthermore, Sarvaśūra, I shall give you another analogy to establish this very point.
Suppose there were a mountain measuring twenty-five *yojanas* in extent and twelve *yojanas* in height.
Then, suppose a certain man were to build a house on the side of that mountain, and after the passing of a long period of one hundred years...
If one were to wipe it once with a garment of Kāśika cloth, by doing so that mountain would be exhausted, yet the *kalpa* would not be exhausted.
This, Sarvaśūra, is the measure of a *kalpa*.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and placed his right knee upon the ground.
Bowing with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was, he said this to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, by means of a single dedication, one produces such a vast mass of merit that,
namely, for eighty eons, one's lifespan will be happy."
"What more need be said of one who will perform even greater service for the teaching of the Tathāgata?
What will be the measure of his lifespan? The Blessed One said: "Listen, son of good family, to the lifespan of one who hears this *Saṃghāṭa* Sūtra."
The lifespan of that person will be eighty-four thousand eons;
what need is there to mention one who causes the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* to be written or recited?
That being, Sarvaśūra, will generate a much greater mass of merit.
O Sarvaśūra, whoever with a serene mind and with resolute intention shall pay homage to the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, he will remember his past lives for ninety-five eons (*kalpa*).
For sixty thousand eons he will be a universal monarch (*cakravartin* king).
O Sarvaśūra, in this very life he will be dear and pleasing to all; furthermore, O Sarvaśūra, he shall not meet his end by means of weapons.
He will become beloved and pleasing; Sarvaśūra, he shall not meet his end by means of a weapon,
nor shall he meet his end by poison, nor by water, nor by fire.
No *kākhorda* demon shall overpower him;
at the time of death, when the final cessation occurs, he will see ninety million Buddhas face to face.
And all those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, O Sarvaśūra, will comfort him.
"Do not fear, O noble son! Since you have heard this well-spoken *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, this great Dharma discourse,
such a mass of merit has been produced by you that ninety-five hundred million Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, residing individually in various world-systems, will bestow prophecies upon you."
What need is there to mention, Sarvaśūra, one who shall hear this *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, this great Dharma-discourse, in its entirety and in detail;
or who shall cause it to be written, recite it, or cultivate it?
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, I shall hear the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, the great Dharma-discourse.
Blessed One, how much of a mass of merit (*puṇyaskandha*) shall I produce?"

The Blessed One said: "Sarvaśūra, that being shall produce a mass of merit equal to the mass of merit produced by honoring as many Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā.
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said: "Blessed One, as I listen to this Dharma-discourse, the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, I do not perceive satiety, O Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, Sarvaśūra, you who do not conceive of satiety regarding the dharmas! I too, Sarvaśūra, do not conceive of satiety regarding the dharmas;
how much less, Sarvaśūra, could foolish ordinary people know satiety?"
[SaSū 34] Any noble son or noble daughter, Sarvaśūra, who shall produce faith in the Mahāyāna,
will not go to a state of ruin for a thousand eons;
for five thousand eons they will not be reborn as an animal.
For twelve thousand kalpas he will possess a corrupt intellect;
for eighteen thousand kalpas he will not be reborn in the border regions;
and for twenty thousand kalpas he will be a hero in giving.
For twenty-five thousand kalpas he will be reborn in the world of the gods;
for thirty-five thousand kalpas he will practice the holy life;
and for forty thousand kalpas he will live as one who has gone forth from the household life.
For fifty thousand kalpas he will be a bearer of the Dharma;
for sixty-five thousand kalpas he will cultivate the recollection of death.
For that son of noble family or daughter of noble family, O Sarvaśūra, no evil deeds whatsoever shall be experienced.
Furthermore, Māra the Evil One will find no opportunity to harm them,
nor shall they ever again be born from the womb of a mother—
those, O Sarvaśūra, who hear this Dharma discourse, the *Saṃghāṭa*.
Wherever they are reborn, there for ninety-five incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) they shall not fall into the lower realms.
For eighty thousand eons they shall be retainers of what they have heard (*śrutadhara*).
For one hundred thousand eons they shall abstain from taking life. For ninety-nine thousand eons they shall abstain from false speech.
For thirteen thousand eons, they will be free from malicious speech.
Sarvaśūra, those beings who shall hear this Dharma-discourse are rare to find.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra rose from his seat and draped his upper robe over one shoulder.
Placing his right knee upon the ground and bowing with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was,
he addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, how much of a heap of demerit will those beings produce?"

"Those who shall reject this Dharma-discourse," the Blessed One said, "will produce a vast heap of demerit from the rejection of the True Dharma, O Sarvaśūra. Sarvaśūra asked: "To what extent, Blessed One, will the heap of evil karma of those beings be?"

The Blessed One said: "Enough, enough, Sarvaśūra! Do not ask me about that mass of evil karma. Rather, Sarvaśūra, listen; I shall explain to you the mass of evil, unwholesome karma of those who reject the true Dharma—how great a mass of evil, unwholesome karma they will take upon themselves."

O Sarvaśūra, whoever rejects this Dharma-discourse, and whoever should give rise to a malicious mind toward twelve times as many Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges, and whoever should reject this *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*— the latter commits a far greater evil than the former.
(When the aggregate of wholesome qualities has appeared, O Sarvaśūra— ) from this they will produce the aggregate of unwholesome qualities.
Therefore, Sarvaśūra, those beings who reject the true Dharma will produce a much greater mass of unwholesome karma than those who give rise to a mind of malice toward the Mahāyāna.
They are burnt, Sarvaśūra; those beings are truly burnt.
Sarvaśūra said: "Blessed One, it is not possible to liberate those beings."
The Blessed One said: "Listen, Sarvaśūra!

It is impossible to release [them]. For example, Sarvaśūra, suppose some man were to cut off the head of a certain being, and then that man were to anoint it with some medicinal ointment, or with honey, or with sugar."

"Or one might smear that head with molasses, or ghee, or oil. What do you think, Sarvaśūra, would it be possible to raise that being back up again? The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said, "It is not possible, Blessed One; it is not possible, Sugata.
The Blessed One said, "In just this way, Sarvaśūra, it is not possible to liberate that being by means of many expedients who has conceived a mind of malice toward the Mahāyāna."
Furthermore, Sarvaśūra,

it is just as if there were a second person who, with a sharp weapon, should strike another being; although he might not be able to deprive that being of life with a single blow, nevertheless, O Sarvaśūra, a wound would still be produced.
Furthermore, when a medicinal treatment is applied, one is then released from the wound;
once released, one then remembers the suffering and thinks:
"I now understand that I shall never again perform the formation of sinful and unwholesome karma."
In the same way, Sarvaśūra, when that person who has rejected the true Dharma remembers the suffering in hell, he then abandons all evil;
and when he abandons all evil,
then he will bring all dharmas before him.
Having brought all dharmas before him,
he will then bring all wholesome dharmas to full completion.
Just as, for example, O Sarvaśūra, the parents of a deceased man grieve and lament, yet [the deceased] does not [receive it].

In this very same way, Sarvaśūra, foolish ordinary beings are unable to protect themselves; they are unable to accomplish their own welfare or the welfare of others, like those who have gone to their parents in despair.
Just so, Sarvaśūra, those beings become hopeless at the time of death.
[SaSū 41] "Sarvaśūra, there are these two things for sentient beings that cause despair at the time of death.
What are the two? Namely, one is a sentient being who performs evil karma or causes it to be performed."
The second, Sarvaśūra, rejects the true Dharma.
These two types of beings are without hope at the time of death.
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra asked: "Venerable Blessed One, what is the destiny of those beings? What is their future state?"

The Blessed One said: "Sarvaśūra, the destiny of those beings who reject the true Dharma is infinite; their future state is endless. Sarvaśūra, for an entire eon they shall experience painful sensations in the Raurava great hell, and for an eon in the Saṃghāta hell."
For one eon in the Tapana hell, for one eon in the Pratāpana hell,
for one eon in the Kālasūtra great hell,
and for one eon in the Mahāvīci great hell.
One eon in the Mahānaraka hell Romaharṣa;
one eon in the Mahānaraka hell Hahe;
(one eon in the Mahānaraka hell Tapana).
Sarvaśūra, beings who have rejected the true Dharma must experience suffering in these eight great hells for eight eons.
[SaSū 43] Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra said this to the Blessed One: “It is suffering, Blessed One; it is suffering, Sugata. I do not venture to hear it.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
(1) Since you do not venture to hear these words of great terror—
how beings experience sensations in hell, which is exclusively suffering—
(2) whatever wholesome karma one performs, happiness shall be his lot.
Whatever unwholesome karma one performs will result only in suffering.
For one who is born, death is suffering; grief is suffering, and then bondage is suffering.
Indeed, suffering is constant for the fool who does not understand the cause of happiness.
(4) Indeed, it is a happiness for the wise who remembers the supreme Buddha;
those who have clear faith in the Mahāyāna will not go to an evil destiny.
(5) In this very way, Sarvaśūra, one is impelled by former karma.
For a small deed is performed, yet an infinite fruit is enjoyed;
just as by sowing a small seed one obtains abundant fruit,
so too in the Buddha-field, from a seed sown in a good field, there is a great harvest.
(7) The wise find happiness and delight in the teaching of the Jina;
they avoid all evils and perform much that is wholesome.
(8) Those who will give even a mere hair’s breadth as a gift within my teaching [shall attain great merit].
For eighty thousand eons, they will possess great enjoyments and vast wealth;
wherever they are reborn, they will always remember their giving.
Thus, indeed, this profound offering to a Buddha yields such great fruit.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra said this to the Blessed One:

"Blessed One, how should the Dharma be understood within the teaching of the Blessed One? Blessed One, having heard the Saṃghāṭa Sūtra, the discourse on Dharma, how will the root of virtue be fully acquired?"

The Blessed One said: "Sarvaśūra, the mass of merit of one who would attend upon as many Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as there are grains of sand in twelve Ganges rivers, providing them with every article of comfort, is to be known as exactly equal to the mass of merit of one who hears this Dharma-discourse, the Saṃghāṭasūtra. The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra asked: "Blessed One, how is the fulfillment of the roots of virtue to be accomplished?"

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra: "Sarvaśūra, that root of merit should be known as equal to the Tathāgata. Sarvaśūra asked: "Blessed One, which root of merit should be known as equal to the Tathāgata? The Blessed One replied:

"Sarvaśūra, the Dharma-preacher (dharmabhāṇaka) should be known as equal to the Tathāgata. Sarvaśūra asked: "Blessed One, who is a Dharma-preacher? The Blessed One replied: "He who [preaches] the *Saṃghāṭa*..."
The Dharma-preacher causes the sutra to be heard.
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said: "Blessed One, those who shall hear this Dharma-discourse, the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, will produce such a mass of merit."
How much more so for those who will write it down (or write it themselves) and recite it? Lord, how great a mass of merit will they produce?
The Blessed One said: "Listen, Sarvaśūra!

Suppose that in each of the four directions there were Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas, as numerous as the sands of twelve Ganges rivers, who remained for twelve kalpas, as numerous as the sands of twelve Ganges rivers, teaching the Dharma to this [person]."
If one were to describe the mass of merit of this Dharma discourse, the *Saṃghāṭasūtra*, for one who writes it down, it would be impossible to reach the limit of that mass of merit,
nor could it be fully expressed by speech; even by Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as numerous as the sands of forty-eight Ganges rivers, it would be impossible to describe while it is being written.
As for that mass of merit, what need is there to mention those who will recite it, or those who will contemplate it, or those who will become meditators on the Dharma?
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra asked: "Blessed One, how much of a mass of merit will they produce by reciting it?"
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:

(10) But when a four-line verse has been recited, whatever merit therein exists— [if] as many Victors (*jina*) as there are grains of sand in eighty-four Ganges rivers were to remain here and describe that merit of what was recited, (11) [they could not exhaust it].
And that merit would not be exhausted until the prophecy were received;

even if eighty million Buddhas were to remain for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges and describe all the qualities of the Mahāyāna in the ten directions, [it would still not be exhausted].
And whatever merit belongs to the *saṃghāṭa* shall never come to an end.
Thus, the teachings of the Dharma by the Buddhas are indeed difficult to encounter and are infinite.
Furthermore, at that time and on that occasion, there were eighty-four hundred thousand *koṭis* of sons of gods.

Bowing with palms joined toward where the Tathāgata was and toward the teaching of the Dharma discourse known as the *Saṃghāṭasūtra*, they said this to the Blessed One: "Excellent, excellent, Blessed One! It is wonderful that such a treasury of Dharma has been established by the Blessed One in Jambudvīpa."

(49) Furthermore, eighteen thousand million Nirgranthas approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they said this to the Blessed One: "Victory to you, O Śramaṇa Gautama! The Blessed One said: "The Tathāgata is always victorious.
"O Nirgrantha heretics, how is it that you, as heretics, speak of victory? They replied: "May the Śramaṇa Gautama indeed be victorious, may he be victorious!"
The Blessed One said: "I do not see victory for you. And he said: (14) "You stand in error; how can there be victory for you? Listen, O Nirgranthas! I shall speak for your benefit."
(15) For one of childish intellect there is no happiness; what victory will there be for you?
I shall show you the profound path through the eye of a Buddha.
[SaSū 50] Then those Nigranthas, in the presence of the Blessed One, became angry and gave rise to a mind of ill-will.
At that time, on that occasion, Śakra, the lord of the gods, was present and seated in that assembly;
seeing those heretical Nigranthas enraged in the presence of the Blessed One, he—
He struck the vajra.
Then those eighteen koṭis of Nigranthas, terrified, trembling, and afflicted by great suffering and dejection, with throats choked by tears, lamented;
and the Tathāgata caused his own self to disappear from view.
Then those Nirgranthas, weeping with tearful faces and no longer seeing the Tathāgata, spoke this verse:
"There is no protector here in this world, neither mother nor father likewise;
we see only a forest here, empty dwellings, and a place devoid of refuge."
There is neither water, nor trees, nor birds;
we see no people here, and being without a protector, we experience a most terrible sensation of suffering, not seeing the Tathāgata.
Who indeed might be a refuge and a protector, by whom one may be rescued from this great fear?
Then, at that time and on that occasion, those eighteen koṭis of Nirgranthas rose from their seats, knelt with both knees upon the ground, and raised their voices, proclaiming this cry:
"The Tathāgata is compassionate, the Perfectly Awakened One, the supreme among bipeds;
grant us benefit and protect this wretched world!"
[SaSū 53] Then the Blessed One, having manifested a smile, addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra:
"Go, Sarvaśūra, and teach the Dharma to the Nigranthas and the followers of other sects.
When this was said, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra said to the Blessed One: "Is it not true, Blessed One, that the Black Mountains bow their peaks before Sumeru, the king of mountains?"
"While the Tathāgata remains present, I shall teach the Dharma.

The Blessed One said: "Enough, noble son; the skillful means of the Tathāgatas are manifold. Go, Sarvaśūra, survey the world-systems in the ten directions and see where you behold the Tathāgata, or where you see the seat of the Tathāgata prepared."
"O Sarvaśūra, I myself shall teach the Dharma to the Nirgranthas and other followers of external paths.
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said: "Venerable Blessed One, by whose miraculous power shall I go? By my own miraculous power, or by yours?"
"Or else, I shall go by means of the supernatural power (*ṛddhyānubhāva*) of the Tathāgata.

The Blessed One said: "Sarvaśūra, go by means of the empowerment of your own power of supernatural transformation (*ṛddhibalādhiṣṭhāna*); and then, Sarvaśūra, come back again by means of the supernatural power of the Tathāgata. Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra rose from his seat.
Having circumambulated the Blessed One, he vanished right there.
[SaSū 55] Then the Blessed One taught the Dharma to those followers of other sects:
"O friends, birth is suffering; birth itself is suffering. For one who is born, many fears arise.
For one who is born, the fear of disease arises; from disease, the fear of old age arises."
In one who is aged, the fear of death arises.
They ask: "Lord, what is the fear of one who is born? The Blessed One said: "It is called 'born, born'."
For a person who has been born, many fears arise: fear of kings arises, fear of thieves arises,
fear of fire arises,
and fear of poison arises.
Fear of water arises;
fear of wind arises;
fear of whirlpools arises.
Fear arises from one's own performed actions.
Thus, while the Blessed One was teaching the Dharma in many ways regarding the cause of birth,
at that time and at that occasion, those non-Buddhist Nigranthas heard it.
A great terror arose, and they said: "O Blessed One, we no longer venture to experience the suffering of birth.

Furthermore, while this *Dharma-paryāya* of the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* was being spoken by the Blessed One, those eighteen koṭis of Nigranthas and followers of other sects became perfected in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment within their own bodies.
And eighteen thousand bodhisattvas, established in the ten great stages,
all displayed various miraculous transformations of their own bodies in many ways, such as the form of a horse.
In the form of an elephant,
the form of a lion, the form of a tiger, the form of a garuḍa, the form of Mount Sumeru, the form of Nandika, and some in the form of a tree—
all of them sat cross-legged upon lotus seats.
Nine thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas sat on the right side of the Blessed One;
nine thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas sat on the left side of the Blessed One.
The Tathāgata, however, being eternally in a state of meditative equipoise, appears to teach the Dharma to sentient beings through his skill in means (*upāyakauśalya*).
For as long as seven days and nights, the Tathāgata extends his palm; and the Blessed One knows that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra is coming here from that world-system Padmottarā.
And when the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra departed, he reached that world-system Padmottarā in seven days and nights through the empowerment of his own supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*).
And when the Blessed One extended his arm,
the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra stood before the Blessed One and circumambulated the Blessed One seven times.
Having circumambulated the Blessed One and with a mind full of serene faith in his presence, he bowed with palms joined toward the Tathāgata and addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, I have traveled to all the world-systems in the ten directions; Blessed One, I have seen ninety-nine thousand billion world-systems."

And, O Blessed One, by my first supernormal power I have seen ninety thousand million Buddha-fields, and by my second supernormal power, a hundred thousand million Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. O Blessed One, I have traveled to all the world-systems in the ten directions; O Blessed One, I have seen ninety-nine thousand million world-systems.

And, Blessed One, by my first supernatural power I beheld ninety thousand *koṭis* of Buddha-fields, and by my second supernatural power, a hundred thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas, the Blessed Ones. Thus, on the seventh day and night, I arrived at that world-system Padmottarā; in the interval, I beheld a thousand *koṭis* of Akṣobhya Buddha-fields, and from there I [beheld] those...
I behold the supernatural power of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones.
In ninety-two hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of Buddha-fields, Tathāgatas are teaching the Dharma.
On that very same day, in eighty hundred thousand kotis of Buddha-fields, eighty hundred thousand kotis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have appeared in the world.
Having paid homage to all those Tathāgatas, I departed once again.
On that very day, Blessed One, having traversed thirty-nine thousand *koṭis* of Buddha-fields,
in each of those thirty-nine thousand *koṭis* of Buddha-fields, there were thirty-nine thousand *koṭis*.

"Blessed One, on the very day those bodhisattvas went forth, they fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; I paid homage to those Blessed Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, circumambulated them three times to the right, and they vanished through their supernatural power. Blessed One, I see Buddhas, Blessed Ones, in sixty billion Buddha-fields."
And I, Blessed One, paid homage to those Buddha-fields and to those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and from there I departed.
Furthermore, Blessed One, in hundreds of millions of other Buddha-fields, I saw Tathāgatas entering final nirvana;
I paid homage to those Tathāgatas as well, and from there I departed.
“Blessed One, I have seen the True Dharma disappearing in ninety-five other *koṭis* of buddha-fields.
Blessed One, mental distress arose within me there, and I shed tears.
Furthermore, I see many others—gods, nāgas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and those capable of changing their form at will—who are weeping and pierced by the great dart of sorrow.”

In this way, another buddha-field was completely consumed by fire, including its oceans, Sumerus, and terrestrial regions; having bowed even to that, O Blessed One, I departed, becoming despondent. Then, O Blessed One, I reached that world-system called Padmottarā, and there, O Blessed One, I saw five hundred thousand millions of seats prepared.
In the southern direction, I see hundreds of thousands of millions of seats prepared;
on my left side, I see hundreds of thousands of millions of seats prepared;
in the eastern direction, I see hundreds of thousands of millions of seats prepared.
In the western direction, I see one hundred thousand times ten million seats prepared;
in the upward direction, I see one hundred thousand times ten million seats prepared.
And, Blessed One, all those seats are made of the seven precious jewels.
And upon all those seats sat Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas, teaching the Dharma.
Thereupon, O Blessed One, filled with wonder, I paid homage to those Tathāgatas and asked them:
"Blessed One, what is the name of this world-system?"
Those Tathāgatas said, "Noble son, this world-system is named Padmottara.
Then, O Blessed One, having circumambulated them, I again questioned those Tathāgatas:
"What is the name of the Tathāgata here in this Buddha-field? Those Tathāgatas replied, "Noble son, he is named Padmagarbha."

"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha who performs the work of a Buddha here in this buddha-field—therefore I said this to them: 'Many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Tathāgatas are seen;
I do not know which one among them is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Padmagarbha.'"

Those Tathāgatas said: "O son of good family, we shall show you that Tathāgata Padmagarbha—him who is the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Padmagarbha. Then, at that very moment, all those bodies of the Tathāgatas vanished, and all the forms of Bodhisattvas appeared.
I saw only a single Tathāgata;
as I bowed my head at the feet of that Tathāgata and stood before him, a seat appeared,
and that Tathāgata spoke to me thus:
"Sit here on this seat, noble son.
Then, O Blessed One, I sat down upon that seat; at that moment, many seats appeared, yet I did not see anyone sitting upon those seats.
"Therefore, I ask the Tathāgata:
'O Blessed One, I do not see even a single sentient being seated upon these thrones. Then the Blessed One spoke to me thus:"

"Noble son, those beings who have not cultivated roots of goodness are unable to sit upon these seats. I then asked that Tathāgata, "Blessed One, what kind of roots of goodness must beings cultivate to sit upon these seats?
He replied to me thus, Blessed One: [text continues]
Listen, noble son: those beings who hear this *Saṃghāṭa* sūtra, this discourse on the Dharma, will, by that root of merit, sit upon these very seats;
what need is there to mention those who will write it down or recite it?
"O Sarvaśūra, because you have heard this Dharma-discourse of the *Saṃghāṭa* and have sat upon this seat—who else in this Buddha-field would grant you entrance within?
When that Blessed One had spoken thus, I said this to the Blessed One: 'Blessed One, how great a mass of merit will that being produce who [hears] this *Saṃghāṭa*? "
He shall hear this Dharma discourse.

Then, at that time, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Padmagarbha, manifested a smile. Therefore, O Blessed One, I asked that Blessed One the reason for his smile: "Who, O Blessed One..."
"What is the cause, what is the reason that the Tathāgata manifests a smile? The Blessed One said:
"Listen, noble son Sarvaśūra, [the bodhisattva mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta]."

"It is just as if, noble son, there were some king who was a universal monarch (cakravartin), the lord of the four continents, and he were to sow sesame seeds in the fields of those four continents. What do you think, Sarvaśūra, would many seeds grow for him? Sarvaśūra replied, "Many, Blessed One; many, Sugata."
The Blessed One said:

"Then, Sarvaśūra, suppose there were a certain being who would make those sesame seeds into a single heap, and another person were to take a single sesame seed from that heap of sesame seeds and place it on the other side. What do you think?"
"Do you think, Sarvaśūra, that a being would be able to count those sesame seeds or to make a comparison?
Sarvaśūra, the Bodhisattva, said: "Certainly not, Blessed One; certainly not, Sugata."
"It is not possible to count those sesame seeds.

The Blessed One said: "In the very same way, Sarvaśūra, it is impossible to provide a comparison for the mass of merit belonging to this Dharma discourse, the *Saṃghāṭa*, except by means of the Tathāgata.
For example, Sarvaśūra, if there were as many Tathāgatas as there are those sesame seeds, and they all [were to describe] this..."

Even if they were to proclaim the merit of the roots of goodness from hearing this *Saṃghāṭa* dharma-discourse, that merit would not be exhausted even by way of analogy; how much more so for one who will write it down or recite it?
The Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said:
“Blessed One, how much merit accrues to one who writes down this Dharma-discourse?
The Blessed One replied:
Listen, son of good family!
Son of good family, it is as if there were a certain man who, in a trichiliocosm great thousandfold world system, were to cut every blade of grass or piece of wood into the size of a finger-joint.
Listen, Sarvaśūra, to a second simile.

It is as if, for example, all the stones, precipices, earth, and even the atoms of dust within the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system were each to become universal monarchs, lords of the four continents, endowed with the seven treasures.
What do you think, Sarvaśūra? Is it not possible to [measure] the mass of merit of all those universal monarchs?
When all sentient beings attempted to provide a simile for it,
the Bodhisattva Sarvaśūra said,
"It is not possible, Blessed One, except for a Tathāgata."

The Blessed One said: "It is even so, Sarvaśūra; it is not possible to make a comparison for the mass of merit produced by writing down this Dharma-discourse of the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*. Greater than the merit of all those universal monarchs (*cakravartin*) is the merit generated by one who writes down even a single syllable from this Dharma-discourse and establishes it."

I shall describe his merit, but not that of those universal monarchs (cakravartin). In the very same way, Sarvaśūra, the merit of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who upholds the true Dharma of the Mahāyāna and abides in its practice cannot be surpassed by universal monarchs; it is just so for him.

The merit arising from the transcription of this *Saṃghāṭa* dharma-discourse cannot be compared by any analogy. O Sarvaśūra, this *Saṃghāṭa* sūtra reveals stores of merit and pacifies all afflictions.
He kindles the torch of all dharmas;
he defeats all the Evil Māras;
and he illuminates the abodes of all bodhisattvas.
He brings forth the accomplishment of all dharmas.

When this had been said, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, in this world, the practice of celibacy is an extremely difficult practice. For what reason? Blessed One, the practice of the Tathāgatas is hard to find."
In this very way, the holy life is difficult to obtain; and when one shall practice the holy life,
then one will behold the Tathāgata face to face,
and there will be the vision of the Tathāgata day and night.
And when he sees the Tathāgata, then he sees the pure buddha-field;
and when he sees the pure buddha-field, then he sees the treasuries of all dharmas.
When he beholds the treasuries of all dharmas,
then at the time of his death no fear arises in him; he shall never again be reborn in a mother’s womb,
and he shall never experience sorrow.

"And he shall not be bound by the snare of craving. When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra: "What do you think, Sarvaśūra? Is the arising of the Tathāgatas not indeed rare? He replied: "It is rare, Blessed One; it is rare, Sugata."
The Blessed One said:

"In this very way, Sarvaśūra, this *Saṃghāṭa* Dharma-discourse is difficult to encounter. Furthermore, Sarvaśūra, those for whom this *Saṃghāṭa* Dharma-discourse comes into the range of their hearing will, for eighty eons, remember their births from birth to birth."
For sixty thousand kalpas he will obtain the sovereignty of a universal monarch;
for eight thousand kalpas he will obtain the status of Śakra;
and for twenty-five thousand kalpas he will be reborn in the company of the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa realm.
For thirty-eight thousand kalpas he will become a Mahābrahmā;
for ninety-nine thousand kalpas he will not go to a state of ruin;
and for a hundred thousand kalpas he will not be reborn among the hungry ghosts.
For twenty-eight thousand kalpas, he will not be reborn among animals;
for thirteen thousand kalpas, he will not be reborn among the asura hosts.
He will not die by the sword, nor by poison, nor by fire, and he shall have no fear of harm from others.
For twenty-five thousand eons he will not be of dull wisdom;
for seven thousand eons he will be one who practices wisdom;
for nine thousand eons he will be handsome and pleasing.
The perfection of his form-body will be just like that of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who is so beautiful to behold.
For fifteen thousand kalpas he shall not be reborn in female form;
for sixteen thousand kalpas no disease shall afflict his body.
For thirty-five thousand divine eons he will possess the divine eye;
for nineteen thousand eons he will not be reborn among the *nāga* species;
and for six thousand eons he will not be overcome by anger.
For seven thousand kalpas he will not be reborn in poor families;
for eighty thousand kalpas he will enjoy two continents.
Even when he becomes poor, he will obtain such happiness as this.
For twelve thousand kalpas he will not be reborn in the wombs of the blind;
for thirteen thousand kalpas he will not be reborn in the states of misery;
and for eleven thousand kalpas he will be a proponent of patience.
At the time of death, when the cessation of the final consciousness is occurring, he will not have perverted perceptions,
nor will he be overcome by anger. He will see before him, face to face, Buddhas, Blessed Ones, equal in number to the sands of twelve Ganges rivers in the eastern direction.
In the southern direction, he will see twenty koṭis of Buddhas face to face;
in the western direction, he will see Buddhas, Blessed Ones, equal in number to the sands of twenty-five Gaṅgā rivers, face to face;
and in the northern direction, he will see Buddhas, Blessed Ones, equal in number to the sands of twenty Gaṅgā rivers, face to face.
In the upward direction, he will see ninety thousand koṭis of Buddha Bhagavats face to face;
in the downward direction, he will see a hundred koṭis of Buddhas Bhagavats, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā, face to face.
And all those Tathāgatas will comfort that son of good family.
"Do not fear, noble son! Having heard this *Saṃghāṭa* discourse on the Dharma, there will be such future benefits and advantages as these.
Do you see, noble son, these many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Tathāgatas, equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā?"
He said, "I see it, Blessed One; I see it, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:
"O noble son, these Tathāgatas have come into your presence for the sake of being seen.
He asked, "What wholesome deed have I performed, by which so many Tathāgatas have come?"
He said: "Listen, noble son! Since you have obtained a human body and the *Saṃghāṭa* Dharma-discourse has come within the range of your hearing, you have thereby generated such a vast mass of merit.
Sarvaśūra said:
“If, Blessed One, such a mass of merit as this belongs to me, what need is there to mention one who hears it in its entirety and completion?
The Blessed One said:
“Enough, noble son! Listen: [the merit of] even a four-line verse (heard).”
I shall describe the merit.

For example, noble son, the mass of merit belonging to as many Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas as there are grains of sand in thirteen Ganges rivers— greater than that mass of merit is the mass of merit of one who hears even a single four-line verse from this Dharma-discourse.
And whoever worships thirteen Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas, equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā,
and whoever hears from this *Saṃghāṭa* Dharma-discourse even a single four-line verse—
this latter person shall produce a much greater mass of merit than that.
How much more so for one who hears it in its entirety and completion!
It is impossible to make a comparison for that mass of merit.
Listen, son of good family, as to what [merit] belongs to one who [hears] this *Saṃghāṭa*—its name is...
He will hear this discourse on the Dharma, this sutra, in its entirety and in detail.

Suppose someone were to sow sesame seeds throughout the entire trichiliocosm, and there were as many universal monarchs (cakravartin) as there were those sesame seeds; then suppose there were a certain man who was wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments.
Then, indeed, that man would give gifts according to their desires to all those universal monarchs.
What do you think, Sarvaśūra, would that man generate much merit on that basis?
He said: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata."

The Blessed One said: "Noble son, whatever mass of merit belongs to all those universal monarchs giving gifts, compared to one who would give a gift to a single stream-enterer, this latter person produces a much greater mass of merit. Even if all the beings in the triple-thousand great-thousand world system were to become stream-enterers, and someone were to give gifts to them all, the mass of merit produced by that person would be greater than that."

One generates a much greater mass of merit by giving a gift to a single once-returner than by giving gifts to all the sentient beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system who were all once-returners;
the mass of merit from giving to all of them is [far surpassed by this].
One generates a much greater mass of merit by giving to a single non-returner than one who gives gifts to all the beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system,
were they all to become non-returners; the mass of merit from giving to all of them is far surpassed by this.

The mass of merit produced by one who gives a gift to a single Arhat is surpassed by the even greater mass of merit produced by one who gives gifts to all the beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system, were they all to become Arhats.

If one were to give gifts to a single pratyekabuddha, and if all the beings in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system were each to become a pratyekabuddha and one were to give gifts to all of them— the mass of merit from that act is far surpassed by the mass of merit produced by one who gives a gift to a single bodhisattva. [This applies even] to those in the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system...
If all the sentient beings in the world-system were to become bodhisattvas, and if one were to give gifts to all of them,
the mass of merit produced from that would be far greater than the mass of merit produced by one who inspires a mind of faith toward a single Tathāgata.

[SaSū 90] Suppose there were someone who would inspire a pure mind toward a trichiliocosm great thousandfold world system filled with Tathāgatas, and suppose there were another who would write down this *Dharmaparyāya* of the *Saṃghāṭasūtra*.
How much more so, Sarvaśūra, regarding one who hears this *Dharmaparyāya*,
and having heard it, upholds it, recites it, masters it, and extensively proclaims it to others?
"What need is there to speak further, Sarvaśūra, regarding those who shall pay homage with a clear mind to this Dharma-discourse, the *Saṃghāṭasūtra*?
What do you think, Sarvaśūra, is it possible for foolish common people to hear this sūtra? He replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One. The Buddha said:
"And those who shall hear it but do not produce faith—
listen, Sarvaśūra, there are some foolish, ordinary beings, Sarvaśūra, who might be able to find the bottom of the great ocean.
He said, "Certainly not, Blessed One."
The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Sarvaśūra, is there any being who could exhaust the ocean with a single palm of his hand? He replied:
"Certainly not, Blessed One; certainly not, Sugata."
The Blessed One said:
"Sarvaśūra, just as there is no sentient being whatsoever who would be able to dry up the great ocean with a single palm of the hand,"

In the same way, Sarvaśūra, those beings who have inferior inclinations are not able to hear this Dharma discourse, nor, Sarvaśūra, are they able to write down this Saṃghāṭa Dharma discourse by those who have not seen hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of Tathāgatas, equal in number to the sands of eighty Ganges rivers.
Those who have not seen Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of ninety Ganges rivers are unable to hear this Dharma-discourse;
those who have not seen hundreds of thousands of millions of Tathāgatas, upon hearing this Dharma-discourse, reject it.

O Sarvaśūra, those who have seen hundreds of millions of Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, upon hearing this Dharma-discourse, give rise to a mind of serene faith and rejoice, seeing things as they truly are.
They understand;
those who, with faith, accept this *saṃghāṭa* discourse on the Dharma as it truly is and do not reject it.
Listen, Sarvaśūra: whoever from this *saṃghāṭa* discourse on the Dharma [retains] even a single syllable or a four-line verse...

Sarvaśūra, after those beings have written down this verse, ninety-five thousand *koṭis* of world-systems beyond that point will be their Buddha-field, just like the world-system Sukhāvatī. And the lifespan of those beings, Sarvaśūra, will be eighty-four thousand *kalpas*.

[SaSū 95] Listen, Sarvaśūra! Those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who shall hear from this *Saṃghāṭa* dharma-discourse even a single four-line verse—listen, Sarvaśūra, suppose there were some being who was fierce, reckless, turned away from the true Dharma, indifferent to the world beyond, and a doer of evil;
one who might commit, cause others to commit, or rejoice in the commission of the five deeds of immediate retribution—if such a person as this...
If one should hear even a single four-line verse from this *Dharma-paryāya* of the *Saṃghāṭa*, those five actions of immediate retribution will be completely exhausted for them.
Listen, Sarvaśūra!
Furthermore, I shall proclaim another quality. Suppose there were some being who would cause the destruction of a stūpa and the schism of the Saṅgha;
who would cause a bodhisattva to fall from meditative concentration, create an obstacle to the Buddha-knowledge, or deprive his mother and father of life.
Then that being, becoming remorseful later on, would grieve and lament: "I am ruined by this body; my future world is lost!
For an eon he would be ruined; consequently, he would experience great mental distress and feel painful sensations;
he would feel bitter sensations.

Sarvaśūra, all beings avoid and loathe that being; they think, "This being is burnt and ruined; he has fallen away from both mundane and supramundane dharmas for many eons, like a charred pillar. In this very way, this person is like a beautifully decorated house whose supporting pillars have been burnt; it no longer shines.
In the same way, this person does not shine in this world;
wherever he goes, there he is reviled by sentient beings and even struck;
though afflicted by hunger and thirst, he obtains nothing at all.
Then he experiences painful sensation.
Due to hunger and thirst, due to verbal abuse, and due to physical blows, he recollects the destruction of stūpas and the five actions of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya*).
Thereupon, he gives rise to a mind of revulsion toward suffering.

"Where shall I go? Who will be my protector? He thinks thus: "I shall go into the mountain caves and glens; there my death will occur, for here I have no protector at all. And he says: "I have committed evil karma; it is like a charred pillar, continuous and unceasing."
"I shall not adorn this world, nor shall I adorn the next; I do not shine within the house, nor do I shine outside. I do not shine anywhere at all, for I am such a doer of evil. (21)
(22) "The evil I have committed because of my faults will cause me to go to a miserable rebirth; suffering there in the next world, where indeed shall I dwell in that miserable state?"
The deities hear his voice as he weeps with a choked throat:
"Alas! Deprived of hope, I shall depart for the next world, for an evil destiny."
The deities said to him:
(24) "You are deluded; go, O man, do not think thus in distress: 'I have no refuge, I have no protector; I experience painful sensations.'"
(25) "I have committed the murder of my mother, the murder of my father, and the five deeds of immediate retribution; I shall go to the summit of the mountain, and from there I will abandon my life.
(26) "Do not go, O foolish man! Do not perform such an evil deed!"
Much evil has been committed by you with a corrupted mind. Those who commit suicide go to hell in suffering;
from there they fall upon the earth, wailing in agony of grief.
(28) By that vigor alone, one does not become a Buddha, nor indeed does one even obtain the vehicle of liberation as a Śrāvaka; therefore,
apply yourself to another kind of vigor.
(29) Go to that mountain retreat where that seer dwells; having gone there and seen that high-souled seer, bow your head at his feet and say: "Be my refuge, O Supreme Being!
Teach me the wholesome Dharma for a moment; I am weary, terrified, and oppressed by excessive suffering. (30)
Then that man, trembling with fear,
went to that mountain where the high-souled Ṛṣi was; having then bowed at the feet of the great seer, (31) he stood there.
(Speaking with a voice that rose up, he uttered these words:
"Out of compassion for me, who am a doer of evil and tormented by the suffering of others, please teach me the Dharma."
(32) "O essence of beings, listen to the seer as he speaks; sit down for a moment and give your attention.
Listen to my words, for I am suffering;
having heard them, consider the means [to remedy it]."
(33) Terrified, trembling, and exceedingly oppressed by suffering, he sat down for a moment. During that brief instant, I confessed the many evils I had committed. Then the seer spoke these words:
The seer said:
(34) "Eat this food which I give you; why do you cry out in pain, oppressed by grief?"
Afflicted by hunger and thirst, you will become hopeless regarding the three realms of existence.
Having offered foods, the seer, seeking to inspire faith in the being, said:
"Eat what is delicious and pleasing, for the sake of satisfying your body."
(36) Afterwards, I shall preach the Dharma that brings about the destruction of all evil; he ate that delicious food for a short while.
(37) Having eaten and washed his hands, he circumambulated the ṛṣi.
Sitting cross-legged, he said: "Whatever evil has been committed—matricide, patricide, and the destruction of a stupa—has been done by me;
an obstacle to the Bodhisattva’s attainment of Buddhahood has been created by me."
(39) Having heard those words of his, the seer then spoke these words: "O man, that which you have done is unwholesome; for you have committed a sinful deed.
(40) Confess the evil karma that was performed by you, whether done by yourself or caused to be done by others."
Then, at that time, that man, pierced by the arrow of grief, frightened, terrified, and agitated, cried out, "Who will be my protector? and he said:
(41) I have committed an evil deed; I shall experience painful sensations in the terrible Raurava hell and likewise in the Pratāpana hell.
Then that man, having prostrated both knees upon the ground before the seer, said:
"I confess the evil karma that was committed and caused to be committed by me;
may its evil fruit not come to pass, and may there be no painful sensation for me."
(43) "The seer shall be my protection; may I be near you, free from remorse and at peace, while my evil deeds are being stilled.
Then, at that time and on that occasion, the seer spoke thus to that man and comforted him in this way.
"Do not fear, son of good family! I shall be your protection; I shall be your refuge and your ultimate resort.
Listen to the Dharma face to face; have you ever heard before the Dharma-discourse named *Saṃghāṭa*?
He replied:
"I have never heard this before.
The seer said, "Who teaches the Dharma to a being who has been consumed by fire, other than one who, dwelling in compassion, teaches the Dharma to beings?
He replied:
Listen, son of good family! Long ago, in the past,
incalculable and even more than incalculable eons ago, at that time and in those days, there was a king named Vimalacandra, a righteous ruler who reigned according to the Dharma.
Furthermore, noble son, a son was born in the house of that King Vimalacandra.

Then King Vimalacandra, having assembled the Brahmins who were experts in the interpretation of marks and omens and learned in the treatises, showed the prince to them and said: "Brahmins, what do you see as the signs of this boy? Are they auspicious or inauspicious?"
Thereupon, a certain Brahmin soothsayer declared, "Great King, this prince who has been born is inauspicious; he is truly inauspicious.
Upon hearing this, the king asked in great agitation, "What is this that the Brahmin soothsayer says? O Lord, if this prince lives for seven years, he will deprive his parents of their lives."
Then that king spoke thus:
"May there be an obstacle to my life rather than my killing my son.
Why is that? Because at some time or other, the birth of a human being is obtained in this world."
"I shall not act in such a way that I will lose this human body.
Then that prince grew; whereas others grow in two years, he grew in a single month.
King Vimalacandra knew that the prince was growing up through the accumulation of his own past karma;
therefore, the king tied the royal fillet upon the prince and spoke thus:
"Let this kingdom be yours; exercise your vast fame, sovereignty, and enjoyments of the realm righteously, and not unrighteously."
Then the king, having bound a turban upon him, gave him the name "Rāja. That King Vimalacandra no longer exercised sovereignty over his own realm.

Thereupon, those thirty million ministers approached King Vimalacandra; having approached, they said this to King Vimalacandra: "Why, O Great King, do you no longer exercise sovereignty over your own realm?"

The king said: "For many incalculable eons, I exercised sovereignty, enjoyment, power, and lordship over kingdoms; yet at no time was there ever satiety for me regarding sense-objects. At that time, on that occasion, after no long interval, that son deprived his parents of life."
And by him, moreover, the five actions of immediate retribution were accumulated there.
Furthermore, O man, I recollect that long period of time as if it were today or tomorrow.
When painful sensations had arisen for that king, he became remorseful and, with a choked throat, lamented, "A sinful deed has been committed by me;

I shall experience painful sensations in the great Avīci hell. Thereupon, having conceived a heart of compassion, I went there and taught the Dharma to that king. Then, having heard that Dharma, that king—[of him...]
Those five deeds of immediate retribution have quickly gone to complete exhaustion without remainder.
And it is said:
"The one of great asceticism [preaches] the *Saṃghāṭa*, the Dharma-discourse, the king of sūtras."
Those who hear this Dharma will attain the unsurpassed state;
all their evils will be exhausted,
and all their afflictions will be stilled.
Listen, I shall proclaim the Dharma by which you will quickly be liberated. By listening continuously while this four-line verse is being recited,
you will bring about the destruction of all evil and become a stream-enterer.
(47) Then I uttered this exalted gift that liberates from all evil;
the suffering beings were liberated from the terrifying fear of hell.
(48) Thereupon that man rose from his seat with palms joined in reverence.
Bowing his head to him, he offers words of praise:
(49) "Excellent! Excellent are the spiritual friends! Excellent is the destroyer of evil!
Excellent is this great method, the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, which those who hear shall [attain]."

[SaSū 106] Then, at that time and on that occasion, twelve thousand sons of the gods stationed in the sky above approached that seer with palms joined in reverence; bowing their heads at his feet, they spoke thus: "O Blessed One, how long do you remember practicing such great austerity? In this way, four koṭis of nāga kings arrived, and eighteen thousand koṭis of yakṣa kings arrived.
Having bowed with palms joined toward where that seer was, they said: "How long do you remember?
The noble seer replied:
"I remember a hundred thousand million billion *niyuta* of incalculable *kalpas*."
He asked:
"By what wholesome deed [is] such evil karma (all evil karma) [eliminated] in a mere moment?"
[He] said, "It is pacified;
having heard the *Saṃghāṭa* discourse on the Dharma,
by this wholesome karma all unwholesome karma has been pacified."

And those beings who were assembled there, by whom this Dharma-discourse was heard and either faith was established or conviction attained— they are all prophesied for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
And by whichever person those five deeds of immediate retribution were committed—

Having heard this Dharma discourse, the *Saṃghāṭa*, in a mere moment those five deeds of immediate retribution were completely exhausted, eliminated, and brought to an end. For him, the doors to all miserable destinies remain closed for many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons,
while the thirty-two doors to the celestial realms are opened wide.

Whoever hears even a single four-line verse from this *Saṃghāṭa* dharma-discourse shall possess such roots of merit; what need is there to mention one who will revere, honor, respect, and worship the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*?

Or, with flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, umbrellas, banners, and flags, or by means of music, the gesture of joined palms, or prostration, they will perform an act of homage; or they will rejoice even once and speak thus:
"Excellent! Well-spoken!"

[SaSū 109] Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how great a mass of merit is produced from a prostration with palms joined by those who, having heard the *Saṃghāṭa* Dharma-discourse being spoken, join their palms and pay homage?

The Blessed One said: "Listen, son of good family, as to how many [merits] are produced by one by whom the five actions of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karmāṇi*) have been committed, caused to be committed, or are being committed."
or even if they have been rejoiced in— if, upon hearing even a single four-line verse from this *Saṃghāṭa* Dharma-discourse, he should join his palms in reverence,
all those five deeds of immediate retribution of his will come to destruction.
How much more so, Sarvaśūra, for one who hears this entire Dharma-discourse in its complete form; he shall produce a mass of merit far greater than that.
Son of good family, I shall provide a simile for you in order to make the meaning of this *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* known.
Sarvaśūra, it is just as if, for example, in the abode of the nāga king Anavatapta, the sun never shines;
yet from there, five great rivers flow forth.
Suppose there were a man who were to count the drops of water in those five great rivers. What do you think, Sarvaśūra, would it be possible by means of counting those drops of water—
To reach the limit [of its measure], he said:
"No indeed, Blessed One; no indeed, Sugata.
The Blessed One said: "In just this way, Sarvaśūra, it is not possible to reach the limit of the root of merit of the Dharma-discourse of the *Saṃghāṭasūtra*."

Whether by means of one eon, or a hundred eons, or a thousand eons, or a hundred thousand eons, or even a hundred thousand *niyutas* of millions of eons, it would be impossible to reach the limit through calculation.
What do you think, Sarvaśūra, is it difficult for one who would proclaim this *Saṃghāṭa* discourse on the Dharma for even a moment?
He said, "It is difficult, Blessed One; it is difficult, Sugata.
The Blessed One said, "Sarvaśūra, even more difficult than that is for one who will be able to hear this Dharma-discourse, the *Saṃghāṭa*, just as [it flows from] the great lake Anavatapta."

Five great rivers flow; it is not possible for any mathematician, nor even a master mathematician, to reach the limit of the number of drops of water in those five flowing great rivers by means of calculation— just so, it is not possible [to calculate] the mass of merit of this Dharma-discourse.
In order to understand the limit [of these], Sarvaśūra asked: "Blessed One, what are those five great rivers?
The Blessed One replied: "They are as follows: the Gaṅgā, the Sītā, the Vakṣu, the Yamunā, and the Candrabhāgā."
Sarvaśūra, these five great rivers enter the great ocean;
and each individual great river has a retinue of five hundred great rivers.

[SaSū 113] Furthermore, Sarvaśūra, these five great rivers flow through the sky, constantly and perpetually flooding the world with their drops of water. Each of these five great rivers has a retinue of a thousand. He asked: "Blessed One, what are those five great rivers with their thousandfold retinues that flow through the sky?"
The Blessed One said: "There is a river named Sundarī with a thousand tributaries,
and a river named Śaṅkhā."
The river named Vahantī has a retinue of one thousand,
and [it is] accompanied by a retinue of one thousand.
The river named Citrasenā has a retinue of one thousand [rivers],
and there is the river named Dharmavṛttā.
O Sarvaśūra, these five great rivers, each with a retinue of a thousand, are those that bring about activity in Jambūdvīpa;
they release showers of rain in drops upon Jambūdvīpa from time to time.
By that [wind], flowers, fruits,
and crops are brought to maturity when showers of rain fall upon Jambūdvīpa.
Then water is produced;
once produced, that water satisfies all fields and groves and brings them happiness.
Just as, O Sarvaśūra, Prajāpati brings happiness to the entire Jambūdvīpa, so it is here.

In this very way, Sarvaśūra, this Saṃghāṭa Dharma-discourse has been proclaimed in Jambūdvīpa for the benefit of many people and for the happiness of many people; yet, Sarvaśūra, as is the lifespan of the Trāyastriṃśa gods, so it is not for humans.
And who, Sarvaśūra, are the Trāyastriṃśa gods, where Śakra, the lord of the gods, dwells?
There are gods named Trāyastriṃśa; for example, Sarvaśūra, those beings who speak even a single word of virtuous speech—
for them, it is impossible to make a comparison for their mass of merit.
[That incomparable happiness which they experience among gods and humans—

] Sarvaśūra, there are beings who utter even a single verbal misdeed; it is impossible to provide a comparison for their sufferings in the hells or as animals, for those beings experience the painful sensations of the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts.
And there is no protector for them; falling into the hells, they lament in despair. This should be understood as being due to the influence of an evil friend.
As for those beings who speak well-conducted speech, it is impossible to make a comparison for their mass of merit.
This should be understood as being due to the influence of a virtuous friend.
When one sees a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), then the Tathāgata is seen;
when one sees the Tathāgata, then all of one's evil deeds are exhausted.
When the destruction of all evil occurs,
then Prajāpati exerts himself for Jambudvīpa;
when Prajāpati exerts himself for Jambudvīpa, [the world flourishes].

At that time, it is impossible to provide even a metaphorical comparison for the happiness of the beings in Jambudvīpa; in this very same way, Sarvaśūra, this Saṃghāṭa Dharma-discourse performs the work of a Buddha for the beings of Jambudvīpa.
At that time, it is impossible to provide a metaphorical comparison for the mass of merit of those beings.
Sarvaśūra, it is just as if there were a place where these five great rivers converge and flow together;
in that place, it is impossible to grasp the measure of the water,
saying it is this many jars of water, or hundreds of jars, or thousands of jars, or hundreds of thousands of jars of water.
Moreover, because of the abundance of water, it receives the designation "a great mass of water.
In the very same way, Sarvaśūra, when the beings of Jambūdvīpa hear this Dharma-discourse of the *Saṃghāta*,
and having heard it, take it up and retain it;
When they shall read it, master it, and extensively proclaim it to others, and when they shall bring it to fulfillment through practice,
then it will not be possible to grasp the measure of the mass of merit of those beings; rather, because of the abundance of that merit, it is reckoned as a "great mass of merit."

[SaSū 119] O Sarvaśūra, those beings who do not hear this *Dharmaparyāya* of the *Saṃghāṭa* will not be able to realize unexcelled, perfect enlightenment; they will not be able to turn the wheel of Dharma; they will not be able to strike the gong of Dharma; and they will not be able to ascend the lion-throne of Dharma. They will not be able to—

It is impossible for those who do not hear this *Saṃghāṭa* Dharma-discourse to enter the realm of *nirvāṇa*, nor can they be illuminated by immeasurable rays of light; Sarvaśūra, it is impossible for them to sit at the seat of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Sarvaśūra said: "I ask, Blessed One; I ask, Sugata."

Out of some curiosity, the Blessed One said: "Ask whatever you desire, Sarvaśūra; I shall remove all your doubts. Sarvaśūra said: "Blessed One, who was that seer by whom those beings were liberated from the five deeds of immediate retribution and established on the stage of non-retrogression? The Blessed One said:
(50) Listen to me, Sarvaśūra, regarding the subtle speech of the Buddhas: the *Saṃghāṭa* Sūtra has been revealed in the form of a ṛṣi.
(51) Out of compassion, the *Saṃghāṭa* reveals the very form of the Buddha.
Just as the Buddha displays his form to Balika on the Gaṅgā,
so too does the Buddha display his form and teach the Dharma himself to whoever desires to see the Buddha, the Protector of the World, the Supreme Victor. (52)
(53) He should listen to the *Saṃghāṭa*; the *Saṃghāṭa* is like the Buddha. Wherever the *Saṃghāṭa* resides, there the Buddha is ever present.
The Blessed One said: "Listen, son of good family!
In the past, Sarvaśūra, I recall ninety-nine incalculable aeons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) ago;
at that time, there appeared twelve billion Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas named Ratnottama. At that time and on that occasion, I was Pradānaśūra."
Their name was Candra.
I attended upon those twelve billion Buddhas with hard foods, soft foods, garlands, perfumes, and ointments, according to their pleasure;

I served them with excellent food and every kind of comfortable provision. Having so served them, O Sarvaśūra, it was right there that I received the prophecy of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
[SaSū 122] Sarvaśūra, I recall that eighteen koṭis of Buddhas, all Tathāgatas named Ratnāvabhāsa, appeared in the world; at that time, I too was there, being Pradānaśūra by name,
and I served and made offerings to those eighteen koṭis of Buddhas.
In whatever manner was appropriate for the Tathāgatas, with perfumes, garlands, ointments, ornaments, and decorations, I received there the prediction of my unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Sarvaśūra, I remember that thirty million Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas named Śikhisaṃbhava appeared in the world.

I honored those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, with worship and respect as was appropriate; and right there I received the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, yet even then the time and occasion for that prediction had not yet arrived.

[SaSū 124] Sarvaśūra, I recall that twenty koṭis of Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas named Kāśyapa appeared in the world; there, I too was Pradānaśūra, and I performed service for those Tathāgatas.
They attended upon the Tathāgatas with perfumes, garlands, and ointments, providing service to the Tathāgatas as great reverence should be shown to them;
and it was there that I received the prediction of my unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Sarvaśūra, I recall that there were sixteen koṭis of Buddhas named Vimalaprabhāsa.
At that time and at that occasion, I was a householder— wealthy,
possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, a renouncer of all possessions (a great relinquisher).
And those sixteen billion Buddhas were honored by me with coverlets and robes, incense, garlands, ointments, ornaments, and clothing.
Just as service to the Tathāgatas ought to be performed, so was it performed by me;
and right there I received the prophecy regarding unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Nor was it the wrong time or the wrong occasion for that prophecy.

Listen, Sarvaśūra! I recall that ninety-five koṭis of Buddhas appeared in the world, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas named Śākyamuni. And at that time, in that era, I was a king, a righteous Dharma-king.
I have attended upon ninety-five koṭis of Tathāgatas named Śākyamuni, honoring them with incense, garlands, ointments, coverlets, robes, and with parasols, banners, and flags;
and it was there that I received the prophecy of my unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
[SaSū 127] Sarvaśūra, I recall that ninety koṭis of Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas named Krakutsanda appeared in the world.
At that time and at that moment, I was a young Brahmin, wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, a giver of gifts who renounced all his own possessions.
And I attended upon all those Tathāgatas with incense, garlands, ointments, rugs, upper garments, ornaments, and coverings.

In whatever manner the service for the Tathāgatas was performed by me—namely, the service rendered to them according to their worth—I received therein the prophecy of my unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; yet there was neither a lapse of time nor an inopportune moment for that prophecy.
Sarvaśūra, I recall that eighteen koṭis of Buddhas appeared in the world;
all were Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas named Kanakamuni. And at that time, in that period, I was Pradānaśūra, and I attended upon those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
They were honored with incense, garlands, ointments, coverlets, robes, and ornaments;

they attended upon me just as they would attend upon the Tathāgatas, my teachers. And there, I received the prophecy of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, yet neither the time nor the occasion for that prophecy had arrived.
[SaSū 129] Sarvaśūra, I recall that thirteen koṭis of Buddhas appeared in the world;
all were Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas named Vabhāsaśiri. I made offerings to those Tathāgatas with rugs, coverings, perfumes, garlands, ointments, garments, and ornaments.
