I attended upon those Tathāgatas with such service as is due to the honoring of Tathāgatas; and by those Tathāgatas, various gateways of the Dharma were [taught].

There, I received the definitive teaching on the meaning and discipline, and I obtained the prophecy of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; yet even now, the time for that prophecy has not arrived. Sarvaśūra, I recall twenty-five koṭis of Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas named Puṣya who appeared in the world.
And at that time, on that occasion, I had gone forth as a renunciant; those Tathāgatas were attended by me just as Ānanda now attends to my service.

In such a manner were those Tathāgatas served by me, and it was right there that I received the prediction of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; yet even until now, the time for that prediction [to be made public] had not arrived.
[SaSū 131] Sarvaśūra, I recall that eighteen *koṭis* of Tathāgatas, Arhats, perfectly enlightened Buddhas named Vipaśyin appeared in the world.
I attended upon those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas with ornaments, garments, clothing, perfumes, garlands, and ointments, just as one should attend upon a Tathāgata.
And at that time, on that occasion, I went forth into homelessness right there.
He received the prophecy of unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, yet even now the time for that prophecy has not arrived; it will not be long before it occurs.
That Vipaśyin, the last to appear in the world, spoke this Dharma-discourse of the *Saṃghāṭa*;
having understood it, at that time I caused a rain of the seven precious jewels to fall upon Jambudvīpa, and then those inhabitants of Jambudvīpa—

The beings there became free from poverty, and it was right there that I received the prophecy of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; yet even now, after such a long period of time, he does not grant me the prophecy [of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena].

[SaSū 133] He asked: "Blessed One, what was that time? What was that occasion? The Blessed One said: "Listen, Sarvaśūra! Then, after two incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Dīpaṃkara appeared in the world.
At that time and on that occasion, Sarvaśūra, I was a young brahmin student (*māṇavaka*) named Megha. And when, Blessed One—"

When the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara appeared in the world, at that time and on that occasion, I also practiced the holy life in the form of a young brahmin. Then, having seen the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, I attained serene faith and scattered seven blue lotuses over him; and I dedicated that root of merit planted before the Tathāgata toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Having dedicated that, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara prophesied: "Young man, in a future time, after incalculable eons, you shall become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Śākyamuni.

Then, Sarvaśūra, standing twelve tālas in the air above the sky, I attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). And as for that which I, Sarvaśūra, [attained] during the incalculable...
Throughout eons, I have practiced celibacy; and whatever roots of merit associated with the perfections I have cultivated, I remember them all as if they were present before me today or tomorrow.
Therein, Sarvaśūra, I established many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings in wholesome dharmas.

How much more so, Sarvaśūra, for me who have now awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment—being compassionate and desiring the welfare of all beings—to teach the dharma of cessation to sentient beings;
such a thing is impossible.
Why is that? Sarvaśūra, it is because I teach the dharma to sentient beings in many different ways.
I teach the Dharma in whatever form is appropriate for beings who are to be disciplined;
in the world of the gods, I teach the Dharma to the gods in the form of a god.
In the abode of the nāgas, in the form of a nāga, I teach the Dharma to the nāgas; in the abode of the yakṣas, in the form of a yakṣa, [I teach the Dharma to the yakṣas].
I teach the Dharma;
in the realm of hungry ghosts, in the form of a hungry ghost, I teach the Dharma to the hungry ghosts.
In the world of humans, I teach the Dharma in human form to humans; to those beings who are to be disciplined by a Buddha, I teach the Dharma in the form of a Buddha.
To those beings who are to be disciplined by a bodhisattva, I teach the Dharma in the form of a bodhisattva;
to those beings who are to be disciplined by a śrāvaka, I teach the Dharma in the form of a śrāvaka.
In whatever form beings may be disciplined, in that very form I teach the Dharma to those beings.

In this way, Sarvaśūra, I teach the Dharma to sentient beings in many different ways. For what reason? Because, Sarvaśūra, just as sentient beings hear the Dharma in many different ways, so too do those who are the essence of sentient beings teach the Dharma to sentient beings in many different ways.
And those beings plant roots of merit in those Tathāgatas;
they give gifts and perform meritorious deeds.
They will be vigilant regarding their own welfare and will cultivate the recollection of death;
they will thus perform such formative actions of wholesome karma.
And by that very same root of merit from hearing the Dharma, they will remember those previous roots of merit.
This will be for their long-term welfare, benefit, and happiness, as well as for that of gods and humans.
For it is thus, Sarvaśūra, that merely upon hearing this Dharma-discourse of the *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*, there arise such immeasurable and incalculable [virtues].
There will be these qualities and benefits.

Then those beings said to one another: "Is there some other wholesome fruit of dharma, through the performance and accumulation of which one awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and becomes a seeker of the welfare of all beings?"
[SaSū 138] Then the Blessed One, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the minds of those beings, said this to them:
"Noble sons, there are those who have faith in the Dharma; they will speak thus: 'The Dharma exists as it truly is.
For them, there will be great fruit, a ripening of happiness, and the unsurpassed bliss of the Dharma."
Those beings who are deluded by ignorance will speak thus:

"There are no phenomena, nor is there anyone who has gone beyond phenomena. For them, there will arise a great fruit with bitter ripening in the states of woe; again and again, those deluded persons [will suffer].
They will be destined for the realms of misery;
for eight eons they will experience the sensation of suffering as hell-beings,
and for twelve eons they will experience the sensation of suffering within the wombs of hungry ghosts.
For sixteen kalpas they will be reborn among the asuras;
for nine thousand kalpas they will be reborn in the wombs of bhūtas and piśācas;
and for fourteen thousand kalpas they will be tongueless.
For sixteen thousand kalpas he will die within his mother’s womb;
for twelve thousand kalpas he will exist as a mere lump of flesh;
and for eleven thousand kalpas he will be born blind.
Experiencing painful sensations,
and having seen one blind from birth,
then the mother and father will think thus:

We have experienced suffering without any reward; our son was born without any reward; for nine months we carried him in our womb, experiencing sensations of cold and heat and undergoing the miseries of hunger and thirst.
Having seen many sufferings to be experienced in this very life, our son was born, yet he has caused neither his mother nor his father to be eager for his sake, nor has he done so for his own body.
Then great despair will arise for their parents.

In the very same way, Sarvaśūra, those beings who reject the true Dharma will be full of despair; destined for the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, at the time of their death they will be pierced by the great dart of grief.

[SaSū 142] Sarvaśūra, those beings who speak such words as "the Dharma exists" and "there is one who has gone to the further shore of the dharmas," by that root of merit will be reborn in Uttarakuru for twenty eons;
they will be reborn in the company of the Trāyastriṃśa gods for twenty-five thousand eons;
and having passed away from among the Trāyastriṃśa gods, they will be reborn in Uttarakuru.
And they shall not be reborn in a mother’s womb;
they shall see hundreds of thousands of world-systems,
and all those world-systems.
Having seen the manifestation of all buddha-fields named Sukhāvatī, they shall establish themselves right there and awaken to enlightenment in that very place.
Thus, O Sarvaśūra, such is the great power of this Dharma discourse, the Saṃghāṭa; those who shall produce a serene faith in it will never pass away through an untimely or violent death.
Those beings will be endowed with perfectly pure morality.
O Sarvaśūra, there are beings who will say: "Day and night, the Tathāgata liberates many beings."
Even now, the realm of sentient beings does not come to exhaustion;
many make the vow for enlightenment,
and many are reborn in the heavenly worlds.
Many attain nirvāṇa;
for what reason, then, is there no exhaustion of sentient beings?
II. Maitreyaparipṛcchā.

[SaSū 145] Then this thought occurred to the other non-Buddhist wanderers, mendicants, and Nirgranthas: "We shall go and engage in debate with the śramaṇa Gautama. Thereupon, ninety-four brahmins, other non-Buddhist wanderers, mendicants, and Nirgranthas [prepared to depart].
And several hundreds of Nirgranthas were approaching the great city of Rājagṛha.
At that time, on that occasion, the Blessed One manifested a smile.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One,
addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, for manifesting this smile?"
"Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not manifest a smile without a cause or a condition.
The Blessed One said: "Listen, son of good family! Today, in this great city of Rājagṛha, a great assembly will take place.
He asked:
“Blessed One, who will come here? Will it be gods, or nāgas, or yakṣas, or humans, or non-humans?
The Blessed One said, “Maitreya, all of these will come here today.”
Gods, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, and non-humans will come here, as will eighty-four thousand brahmins;
ninety thousand koṭis of heretics, wandering mendicants, parivrājakas, and nirgranthas will also come here.
They will engage in debate with me.
To pacify the disputes of them all, I shall teach the Dharma;
and all those brahmins will generate the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, nine hundred billion followers of other sects—carakas, parivrājakas, and nirgranthas—all shall attain the fruit of stream-entry.
Eighteen thousand million nāga kings will come;
they shall hear the Dharma from me, and having heard it, they—
All will generate the resolve for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Sixty thousand billion sons of the gods from the Śuddhāvāsa realm will come;
thirty-two thousand million Māras, the Evil Ones, together with their retinues, will also arrive.
Twelve thousand koṭis of asura kings will come,
and about five hundred kings, together with their retinues, will arrive to hear the Dharma.
Having heard the Dharma from me, they will all resolve their minds upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and circumambulated the Blessed One three times, vanished right there.

III. Sarvaśūraparipṛcchā (2) [SaSū 152] Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One.
He said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what are the names of these five hundred kings?
The Blessed One said: "Listen, Sarvaśūra! There is a king named Nanda, a king named Sunanda, and a king named Upananda."
A king named Jinarṣabha;
a king named Brahmasena;
a king named Brahmaghoṣa.
The king named Sudarśana;
the king named Jayasena;
the king named Nandasena.
King Bimbisāra by name,
King Prasenajit by name,
and King Virūḍhaka by name.
Led by these, there were approximately five hundred kings,
each king accompanied by a retinue of two hundred thousand koṭis; they had all set out for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment— with the exception of King Virūḍhaka—
from the eastern direction, thirty thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas arrived.
From the southern direction, fifty thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas arrive;
from the western direction, sixty thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas arrive;
and from the northern direction, eighty thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas arrive.
From the downward direction, ninety thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas arrive;
from the upward direction, one hundred thousand koṭis of bodhisattvas arrive;
and all of them are established upon the ten stages.
Then all those bodhisattvas approached the great city of Rājagṛha, the Vulture Peak Mountain, and where the Blessed One was, in order to see and pay homage to the Blessed One.
All those bodhisattvas had set out for unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra:
"Go, Sarvaśūra, and speak thus to the Bodhisattvas in all the world-systems throughout the ten directions:
'Today the Tathāgata is teaching the Dharma in the great city of Rājagṛha.'"
"Therefore, all of you who reside in the world-systems of the ten directions, join your palms in reverence;
and having heard this, return once more in a mere moment to listen to the Dharma.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra rose from his seat, bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, and [addressed] the Blessed One...
Having circumambulated [the Buddha], he vanished by means of his supernatural power.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra went to the world-systems in the ten directions and announced to the Bodhisattvas:
"Friends, today the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, is teaching the Dharma to sentient beings in the great city of Rājagṛha within the Sahā world-system."
"Therefore, you should grant your approval;
this will bring you benefit, happiness, and great gain this very day.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra, having gone to the world-systems in the ten directions and attended upon all the Buddhas, announced this to the Bodhisattvas.

Just as a strong man might snap his fingers, in that very instant the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra came from the great city of Rājagṛha to where the Blessed One was, and having arrived, he stood before the Blessed One;
and there all the brahmins, followers of other sects, wanderers, mendicants, and Nirgranthas had assembled.
Many gods, nāgas, humans, and non-humans, as well as about five hundred kings together with their retinues, had assembled;

and thirty-three thousand koṭis of Māras, the Evil Ones, together with their retinues, had also assembled. Then, at that time, the great city of Rājagṛha trembled, and divine sandalwood powder rained down throughout the world-systems in the ten directions.

A divine rain of flowers fell, and it formed a gabled pavilion above the crown of the Blessed One’s head. Furthermore, at that time, Śakra, the lord of the gods, struck his vajra in front of the Tathāgata.
Then, at that very moment, four great winds from the four directions arose in agitation and blew forth.
And whatever refuse, dust, or gravel there was in the great city of Rājagṛha, they all cast outside the city;
they caused a rain of fragrant water to fall throughout the world-systems in the ten directions;
and they caused a rain of blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses to fall throughout the world-systems in the ten directions.
And those flowers remained as flower-parasols above the heads of those beings;
and above the head of the Tathāgata, in the sky overhead, eighty-four thousand gabled pavilions were established.
Within those eighty-four thousand flower-gabled pavilions, eighty-four thousand seats made of the seven precious gems appeared, having been prepared.
And on every seat, the Tathāgata sat and taught the Dharma;
then indeed, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
[SaSū 162] Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvaśūra, having bowed with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was,
addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, for such miraculous displays as these occurring in the great city of Rājagṛha?"
[They] appear.

The Blessed One said: "Suppose, for example, there were a certain man who was fickle and frivolous, established in the notions of 'I' and 'mine,' and he were poor; yet the king might stroke his head. Then, out of excessive pride, that man [would go] as far as the royal gate."
If, having gone there, he should wish to enter that royal palace by force, then those ministers and courtiers of the king would seize that man and beat him in many ways.
Then, at that time and on that occasion, the king should hear this report: "This poor man desires to enter the interior by force."

Upon hearing this, he would certainly think, "This man surely intends to have me killed. Then the king, enraged, would say to his attendants: "Go, sirs, take this man to a mountain cave and deprive him of life;
bring ruin upon his entire retinue, including his parents, sons, daughters, female and male slaves, and laborers."
Then, if all of them were deprived of life, all his kinsmen and circle of relatives would be pierced by the dart of supreme sorrow;
in the very same way, Sarvaśūra, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, teaches the Dharma to sentient beings.

In this regard, just as that man was conceited, so too do foolish ordinary people perceive the Tathāgata by grasping at signs—such as form, color, marks, and shape—and conceive of him as "the body of the Tathāgata. Having heard many teachings therein, they fall into conceit and utter various idle prattle; these beings are overwhelmed by the notions of "I" and "mine."
They do not listen to the Dharma themselves, nor do they proclaim it;
yet if anyone should announce to them even a single sutra, a verse, or at least a parable,
they do not grasp it and do not lend an ear.
"We know this ourselves.
For what reason? Because of their excessive pride, they fall into negligence despite their great learning, as they associate with foolish worldlings.
They will not hear such speech endowed with the Dharma;
through that great learning they will become negligent,
and those men of such a kind will establish their own poetic compositions.
They establish their own compositions as gifts;
they bring ruin to the entire world and to themselves,
and they will consume in vain the abundant alms provided by the kingdom.
And having eaten, they will not properly digest it;
and at the time of their death, there will be great terror for them,
and those beings will say this to him:
"Many of us have been taught the knowledge of crafts by you; how is it that you are not able to sustain yourself?
He would say to them, "Friends, it is not possible for me to sustain myself at this time.
Thereupon, those beings, having heard what he had said...
They will lament in various ways, just as for the sake of that one individual, many assemblies of kinsmen were deprived of life though they were innocent, due to the condition of their own karma;
in the same way, at the time of death, those beings, while lamenting for them, will see themselves destined for the realms of hell and the animal birth.
Observing this, I say the same to you Brahmins, as well as to the other sectarians—the Carakas, Parivrājakas, and Nirgranthas—on account of your unwholesome friends:
"Do not be negligent! Just as a bird whose wings have not yet grown is unable to traverse the sky to reach the world of the gods, even so it is for you who abide in the notions of 'I' and 'mine'."
"It is not possible for you to attain nirvāṇa, nor does such supernatural power exist among you.
Why is that? Because by way of your karma, you have been born like those of the chicken womb; before long, this body, subject to disintegration, will reach its end in death.
At the time of death, there will be a lack of relish and a state of great distress."
"Why have we sustained this physical existence, we who shall neither experience the happiness of the gods nor the happiness of the human world,
nor shall we abide in the state of nirvāṇa? Our bodies have been borne in vain."
What will be our destination, and what will be our final resort?
Where will there be rebirth, and where will there be cessation?
Then the Blessed One addressed those other sectarians, wandering mendicants, naked ascetics, and brahmins once again.
"Friends, do not become hopeless regarding this Jambudvīpa made of jewels;
do not be excluded from this jewel of the Dharma.
Ask the Tathāgata whatever you desire, friends, and I shall fulfill all your intentions."

[SaSū 171] Then all those brahmins, followers of other sects, carakas, parivrājakas, and nirgranthas rose from their seats, draped their robes over one shoulder, joined their palms in reverence, and questioned the Blessed One: "Blessed One,
day and night the Tathāgata liberates many sentient beings from saṃsāra."
Nor is there any diminution or increase of the realm of sentient beings perceived.
Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, that these sentient beings, being equal [in nature], manifest arising and cessation?
(The Inquiry of Sarvaśūra in the Great Dharma Discourse of the *Saṃghāṭa* is completed.)
IV. The Questions of Bhaiṣajyasena.
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena:
“The followers of other paths gird themselves with a great armor.”
For the sake of dispelling great remorse,
and for the purpose of kindling the great torch of the Dharma,
they inquire about the cause of this great question.

"Listen, sons of good family! Here, the element of earth, the element of water, the element of fire, and the element of air are infinite and boundless; yet the realm of sentient beings is even more infinite than these. There are sentient beings who, for the sake of the welfare of beings, will appear in the final age to [teach] arising and cessation—beings whether young or old who will bring about arising and cessation. Bhaiṣajyasena, there are aged beings who, like children, do not know anything at all."
Bhaiṣajyasena, it is just as if, for example, a certain man were to wash his head and put on new clothes, and then go out from his house;
and people would address him, saying,
"Your new clothes are well-donned."
Then suppose there were another being who would wash his head and wash his old clothes; having washed them, he would put them on, but they would become loose and not look beautiful.
That man’s head would be well-washed, yet his clothing would not be handsome.
In the same way, Bhaiṣajyasena, there are aged beings who do not adorn Jambūdvīpa,
whereas young beings display arising and passing away.
Then, all those heterodox practitioners, wandering mendicants, naked ascetics, and brahmins rose from their seats.
They said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, who among us is old and who is young? The Blessed One said:
"You are all old, for having repeatedly witnessed the painful sensations in the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, even until today you have not attained satiety.
Then indeed, all those brahmins, heterodox practitioners, wandering mendicants, and naked ascetics—all of them—[spoke].

And the nāga kings said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, we no longer venture to experience painful sensations within saṃsāra. And those other heterodox practitioners—carakas, parivrājakas, nirgranthas, and brāhmaṇas—spoke thus: "There are no young beings who are capable of realizing the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā)."
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena said this to the Blessed One:
"Behold, Blessed Lord, how difficult it is for these beings to have faith! The Blessed One said: "Listen, Bhaiṣajyasena;
now the Tathāgata shall make it manifest before the eyes of the whole world."

[SaSū 177] Then, ninety-four thousand koṭis of young beings stood before the Tathāgata; yet they did not bow to the Tathāgata, nor did they speak to him, nor converse with him, but remained silent, accepting him through their silence.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, who are these?"
"What is the cause, what is the condition, that these beings do not address the Blessed One, do not converse with him, do not pay him homage, and do not question the Blessed One?
The Blessed One said: "Listen, Bhaiṣajyasena! Those beings who say, 'It is not possible for new beings to directly realize the true nature of phenomena (dharmatā),' [are the reason]."
"Bhaiṣajyasena, you should look upon these beings as novices. And those beings said, 'Venerable Blessed One, we are novice beings; Venerable Sugata, we are novice beings.
The Blessed One said, 'O beings, now demonstrate to the world the measure of your own bodies before the eyes of the world.'"

Furthermore, at that time and on that occasion, ninety-four thousand koṭis of new beings, upon the dissolution of their bodies, remained in the intermediate space and attained the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena said this to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, it is a great gain to have such as these."

Those beings who exert vigor for the exhaustion and complete termination of saṃsāra—O Blessed One, it is as if these beings have arisen this very day; O Blessed One, it is as if these beings have been fully liberated this very day; indeed, all are seen this very day established upon the ten stages.

[SaSū 179] Then all the brahmins, the followers of other sects, the carakas, the parivrājakas, and the nirgranthas, as well as the nāga kings and Māra the Evil One with his retinue, approached in order to deprive him of his sight.
And they all said this to the Blessed One: "Lord, we have come here into the presence of the Tathāgata in order to deprive him of his sight.
But having heard this Dharma discourse, Lord, we have obtained serene confidence in the Buddha and in the Dharma."
In that regard, O Blessed One, may all of us likewise obtain such a Buddha-happiness as this, O Blessed One.
"May we likewise become Tathāgatas, Arhats, and perfectly enlightened Buddhas in the world.

The Blessed One said, "It is so, gentle sirs; it is just as you have come into the presence of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha. Having heard this Dharma discourse, the *Saṃghāṭa*, you have generated the resolve for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
"By this root of merit, O gentle-faced ones, you shall before long realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete awakening. As soon as these words were spoken by the Blessed One,
at that very moment, all those heterodox practitioners, wandering mendicants, ascetics, and brahmins attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

And all became bodhisattvas established on the ten stages; and all those bodhisattvas, having risen into the air to the height of seven palm trees, offered gabled palaces made of the seven precious gems to the Tathāgata.
And they all performed various miraculous transformations, empowerments, and supernatural feats.
Then, at that very moment, they all stood above the head of the Blessed One and scattered various flowers over the Blessed One;

they brought the Tathāgatas to mind and conceived the perception of the Buddha within their own bodies, along with many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sons of gods [with divine flowers].
They scattered [offerings] over the Tathāgata and spoke these words:
"Great is the gain for the Śramaṇa Gautama! Great is the field, the Lord of the World, who has attained the empowerment of the power of meditative concentration and is wise."

One who seeks the welfare of others— that is, one who liberates such beings from cyclic existence gradually through skillful means— by means of a single well-spoken word, so many beings are liberated from cyclic existence.

[SaSū 183] Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and bowing with palms joined toward the Blessed One,
addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason, that these sons of the gods utter such words?"
They performed many meritorious acts of volitional formation and praised the Tathāgata with many hymns of praise for his virtues.
The Blessed One said: "Listen, son of good family; they are not praising me."
They praise their very own bodies;
they will establish their very own bodies upon the throne of the Dharma King; they will establish their very own bodies upon the seat of the supreme Dharma.
They will emit rays of Dharma from their very own bodies;
they will be sustained by all the Buddhas for the sake of awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, and having awakened, they will teach the Dharma.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable Blessed One, many beings; Venerable Sugata, many beings are liberated day and night, yet even now there is no exhaustion of beings."
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, Bhaiṣajyasena! It is well that you consider this matter to be asked of the Tathāgata.

Listen, Bhaiṣajyasena. For example, Bhaiṣajyasena, suppose there were a certain man who was wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments, with abundant wealth, grain, treasuries, and storehouses, and who possessed many male and female slaves, laborers, and servants."

Suppose he possessed many heaps of wealth, many fields and groves, and much grain and money— such as barley, wheat, rice, sesame, beans, mung beans, and so forth— and that man, during the springtime, would sow all that grain and money. Then, after some time, when all that grain and money had ripened, he, knowing them to be ripe, would have them brought into his inner house.
That man stores those riches and grains separately within the house; having stored them,
he enjoys them until the time of spring arrives.
Once again, he sows those very seeds.

In the same way, Bhaiṣajyasena, these sentient beings, having previously performed virtuous deeds, later, upon the exhaustion of those deeds, repeatedly seek a field of merit, plant roots of goodness, and having planted those roots of goodness, they practice and accomplish those wholesome dharmas therein.
Those endowed with correct practice cause all dharmas to increase;
having caused all dharmas to increase, they give rise to joy and rapture.
And by that mind of joy and rapture, Bhaiṣajyasena, they are not destroyed for many thousands of millions of eons.
In the same way, Bhaiṣajyasena, a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening (prathamacittotpādika) never possesses a nature subject to destruction.
In brief, he understands all phenomena.
He asked: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening see a dream?"
The Blessed One said:
"Bhaiṣajyasena, a bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening sees many fears within his dreams.
For what reason? It is because when he sees fears within his dreams,"
At that time, one purifies all sinful karmas.
Bhaiṣajyasena, it is not possible for a sentient being with sinful karma to remove intense suffering; nor does fear arise in him from seeing a sinful dream.
Bhaiṣajyasena asked: "Blessed One, what kinds of fears does a bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening see within a dream?"
The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, he sees a blazing fire.
There, that bodhisattva should generate this thought: 'All my afflictions have been burned away. Second, Bhaiṣajyasena, he sees water that is turbid and thoroughly churned.
There, that bodhisattva who has first generated the thought of awakening must not be discouraged."
For what reason? Because, Bhaiṣajyasena, when a bodhisattva has thus turned back all the bonds of delusion, he has brought about the destruction of all evil.
Bhaiṣajyasena, thirdly, a bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening sees a dream of great terror. He asked: "Which one, Blessed One?"
The Blessed One said: "He sees his own head shaven on his body.

In that regard, Bhaiṣajyasena, that bodhisattva who has first produced the thought of awakening must not feel dejected. Why is that? He should produce this thought: 'My passion, hatred, and delusion have been shaven away.'"
And my saṃsāra of the six realms of existence will be conquered;
for there will be no dwelling in hell for him, nor among animals, nor among hungry ghosts.
Bhaiṣajyasena, a bodhisattva who has first resolved upon awakening does not take rebirth among the asuras, nor among the nāgas, nor even among the pure buddha-fields of the gods.
(This shall be so.)
Bhaiṣajyasena, in the future time, in the final age, if any sentient being should direct their mind toward awakening,
they should expect great revilement and they will dwell in contempt.
In this regard, Bhaiṣajyasena, a bodhisattva who has first resolved his mind upon awakening should not give rise to a mind of weariness, nor should he be discouraged.

Bhaiṣajyasena, many teachings have been taught by me; and Bhaiṣajyasena, for many hundreds of thousands of millions of eons, I have practiced difficult austerities. Bhaiṣajyasena, it was not for the sake of royal enjoyments, nor for the sake of livelihood or worldly pleasures that I did so.

"Bhaiṣajyasena, I have practiced austerities for the sake of sovereign power and enjoyments, or I have practiced austerities for the sake of awakening to the nature of phenomena; yet, Bhaiṣajyasena, I did not fully awaken to unsurpassed,
perfect enlightenment as long as I had not heard this Dharma discourse, this *Saṃghāṭa*, at the time when it was heard by me."

On that very day, Bhaiṣajyasena, this profound Dharma discourse was heard by me, and I attained unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. This Dharma discourse, Bhaiṣajyasena, is deep; its hearing is difficult to obtain even in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons.
Bhaiṣajyasena, the appearance of Tathāgatas is extremely rare; Bhaiṣajyasena, the hearing of this [Dharma] is extremely rare.
The upholder of this Dharma-discourse—
those who shall hear this Dharma-discourse,
all of them will fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Bhaiṣajyasena, for hundreds of thousands of eons, sentient beings will turn their backs on saṃsāra;
they will obtain a perfectly pure buddha-field and realize the path to cessation.
They are capable of discerning the basis;
they are capable of discerning the ground of the wholesome;
they are capable of discerning the ground of the wholesome pertaining to the higher knowledges; they are capable of discerning the cessation of the ground of the wholesome.
[Bhaiṣajyasena asked: “For what purpose, Bhaiṣajyasena, is cessation itself spoken of?
He replied:
“It is spoken of for the sake of the meaning, O Blessed One; it is the station of the Dharma. The Blessed One said: “What, Bhaiṣajyasena, is the station of the Dharma?”
He said: "Blessed One, 'Dharma' refers to the exertion of vigor and the undertaking of ethical discipline."
The possession of ethical discipline is called the treasury of the Dharma.
"Blessed One, this treasury of the Dharma comes into being.
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, Bhaiṣajyasena, you who..."
"You think that this matter should be asked of the Tathāgata.
He said, "For what reason, Blessed One, do the Tathāgatas arise in the world?
The Blessed One said, "Bhaiṣajyasena, it is because they understand the possession of great learning."
They understand the arising of the Tathāgatas;
having understood the arising of the Tathāgatas, they understand this state of bliss that is the arising of the Tathāgatas.
And when the Tathāgatas arise in the world, then sentient beings understand all phenomena.
They understand the dharmas of skillful means;
they understand mundane and supramundane dharmas;
they understand mundane and supramundane gnoses.
[SaSū 194] He asked: "Having known gnosis in this way, what do they understand as nirvāṇa?
The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, they understand the Dharma itself;
having understood the Dharma itself, [they understand it] in just this way."
Bhaiṣajyasena, for those who understand the compendium of the Dharma, the first gain arises;
by taking up what has been heard, there will be only a righteous gain.
Bhaiṣajyasena, it is just as if some man were a merchant, and he were traveling for the sake of profit.

Suppose a person were to take a thousand man-loads of gold, both his own and that belonging to others, and set out on his way. As he was departing, his mother and father said to him: "Listen, noble son! This thousand man-loads of gold has been taken, both your own and that of others. You must handle this gold with great care; you must not let even a fraction of it be lost. Having secured a great profit, ensure that the gold itself is well-secured, for that will bring us great profit."
"We shall live happily, and that son will speak thus to his parents: 'I shall do so.
Having said this, the merchant would take the gold and depart. Then, through negligence, within a mere month, that merchant might destroy all the gold and bring it to ruin.
Thereupon, that man, overcome by extreme anxiety and with a heart pierced by the arrow of grief, would not enter his own home out of shame and fear."

If his parents were to hear that all that gold had been destroyed by their son, they would become despondent; with their hearts struck by the arrow of grief, they would tear their clothes, lament, wail, and thus bewail:
"A wicked son has been born in our house in the form of a son, and he has destroyed the entire household!"
Having rendered us helpless, they were made into slaves and laborers;

their parents, their hearts overcome by anxiety and having lost all hope, passed away. Then that son heard that his parents had passed away in despair, and he too, being equally despondent, passed away.
"In the same way, Bhaiṣajyasena, the Tathāgata also speaks this matter:
those beings who do not have faith in my teaching become hopeless; at the time of death, their hearts struck by the arrow of grief, they pass away excluded from the great jewel of the Dharma.

Just as those two parents, hopeless and lamenting for the sake of the gold, their hearts struck by the arrow of grief, fall into anxiety, being possessed by the arrow of grief over the gold—whether belonging to another or to themselves."
In the very same way, Bhaiṣajyasena, those who have no faith in my teaching, later, at the time of death, being tormented and lamenting, experience painful sensations;
having exhausted the merits previously performed, they do not further create other merits that reside in a fertile field.

There, for them whose merit is exhausted and whose hearts are pierced by the thorn of grief, at that time and on that occasion, seeing the terrible and dreadful rebirths in the hells, the animal realm, and the world of Yama, at the time of death—
Thus he thinks:
"Who might be my protector, so that I may not see the realm of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and the world of Yama, and may not experience those painful sensations?"
[SaSū 199] As he was thus lamenting and departing for the next world, his parents spoke to him in this way: "What shall we do, dear son? And they addressed him with these verses:
(54) "This disease, this suffering, this great terror cannot at all be grasped."
"There is no death for you, my son; for one who is ill, there is fear of death.
But liberation from this terrifying and fearful disease shall come to you.
Take heart, my son; from that, success will follow."
The son said:
(56) "My consciousness is ceasing; my body is being severely tormented; all my limbs are in pain; I see death before me."
(57) My eyes do not see, nor do my ears hear;
I shall no longer obtain the faculty of hearing, and my body will not endure. (58) My limbs and members ache like senseless pieces of wood.
"You are deceiving me, mother; death has not yet come for you.
The mother said:
"You ought not to speak thus, my son; do not make me fall into a state of terror."
"You see your body overcome by fever and various afflictions.
The son said:
"I do not see fever in my body, nor disease, nor do I suffer."
I behold death, terrible, and my body is utterly struck down. I see my entire self, my whole body, tormented by suffering;
to whom shall I go for refuge? Who will be my protector?
(62) The parents said to their son: "Indeed, divine wrath will befall you; therefore, having performed a sacrifice to the gods, thereupon well-being will come to pass. The son replied:

(63) "You yourselves must do that by which my well-being may be secured; go very quickly, indeed, and ask Devapālaka. Then his parents, having gone to Devakūṭa, caused incense to be offered to the god.
Then that temple guardian, having offered incense to the god, spoke these words:
"The god is angry with you; you must perform service for the god and conduct a sacrifice.
Therein, an animal must be slaughtered and a human must also be slaughtered; then your son will be delivered from his illness."
Then, at that very moment, the parents thought to themselves: "What shall we do? We are poor.
If the King does not grant his favor, our son will die;
yet if he should show us grace, we are so utterly destitute that we must bring him a sacrificial animal and a human being."

[SaSū 201] Then, having gone very quickly to their own home, they sold whatever household goods were available there; they went for the purpose of buying livestock. Then, they spoke thus to a certain man: "O man, give us gold that we have requested; if we are able to repay it again on the tenth day, that would be excellent."

"We are unable to give it; therefore, we shall become your slaves and laborers. Then, having taken that gold, the two of them would go to purchase livestock and a man. Now, once they have purchased the livestock and the man, that man would not know that "these people will deprive me of my life."
Then those two parents, having fallen into a state of delusion, did not enter their own home again;
they went to the temple and addressed the temple-attendant:
"Perform the sacrifice quickly now!"

Then those parents themselves caused that animal to be slaughtered and deprived that man of his life. Thereupon, as the deity-protector was about to sacrifice the fat for the sake of performing the sacrifice, that deity descended and spoke thus:
"Your son has been taken by me."

Then those parents, overflowing with love and joy, said: "It would be better if our son were to live; we shall become his servants. Having thus turned back and performed a grand sacrifice to the deity, they went to their own home, where they then saw that their son had passed away.

Then those two parents, their hearts pierced by the arrow of grief through great suffering and despondency, became hopeless and passed away right there. In this very way, Bhaiṣajyasena, should one regard the association with unwholesome friends.
He said: "I ask, Blessed One; I ask, Sugata. He replied:
"Ask, Bhaiṣajyasena."
He asked: "Blessed One, where is the rebirth of those beings, and what is their future destiny? He replied:
"Enough, Bhaiṣajyasena; what is the use of your asking about this matter?"
He said:
"I ask, Blessed One; I ask, Sugata.
The Blessed One said:
In that regard, Bhaiṣajyasena, the mother was reborn in the great hell Raurava;

the father was reborn in the great hell Saṃghāta; the son was reborn in the great hell Tapana; and Devapālaka was reborn in the great hell Mahāvici. He asked: "Blessed One, where is a person who has committed no offense reborn? What is his future destiny?"
The Blessed One said: "In this case, Bhaiṣajyasena, it should be understood that the man who was innocent will be reborn into the company of the Trāyastriṃśa gods. He asked:
"Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, by which that man is reborn into the company of the Trāyastriṃśa gods?
The Blessed One said: "Listen, Bhaiṣajyasena. At the time of his death, while being deprived of life, that man [directed his mind] toward the Tathāgata."

Having thus clarified his mind, he spoke these words: "Homage to that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One! Having uttered this once, Bhaiṣajyasena, by that root of merit, he will experience the happiness of the Trāyastriṃśa gods for sixty eons;
for eighty eons, he will remember his births from birth to birth.
In every birth he shall be free from all sorrow;
as soon as he is born, he shall extinguish all sufferings.
Indeed, it is not possible for you to bring all sentient beings to final nirvana.
When this had been said, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena addressed the Blessed One as follows:

“Blessed One, how is it that all sentient beings cannot be led to final nirvāṇa? The Blessed One replied: “Bhaiṣajyasena, one must exert diligence. He asked: “Blessed One, what is the exertion of diligence? The Blessed One replied:
Listen, Bhaiṣajyasena, what is called "vigor" is the manifestation of fruits;
namely, that which is called the fruit of stream-entry is a station of vigor,
and that which is called the fruit of once-returning is a station of vigor.
The fruit of non-returning is called a station of vigor;
the fruit of arhatship and the cessation of an arhat are called a station of vigor;
the fruit of a pratyekabuddha and the knowledge of the fruit of a pratyekabuddha are called a station of vigor.
The fruit of the bodhisattva stages is the station of awakening, called the station of vigor.
These, Bhaiṣajyasena, are the names of the stations of vigor.
He asked: "Blessed One, how should one demonstrate the stream-enterer and the fruit of stream-entry?"
The Blessed One said:
"Bhaiṣajyasena, it is just as if some man were to plant a tree;
on that very day, a sprout would grow from the planted tree."
On the very day that the sprout had grown, on that same day it would sink one *yojana* beneath the surface; and suppose another man were likewise to plant a tree,
but then, on that very same day, due to the agitation of the wind, no sprouts of that tree grew, and so that man [would depart] from there.
He would uproot that tree from its place; then another man would engage in quarreling, scolding, strife, and dispute, saying, "For what purpose are you digging up my land?
At that time and on that occasion, the king heard that two men had become engaged in mutual quarreling, scolding, strife, and dispute.

Because of that dispute, the king dispatched a messenger to them, saying, "Go, my man, bring those two men here. "As you command, Your Majesty," that man replied to the king and, hurrying along, approached those two men and said to them, "The king summons you both. Then, at that very moment, one man there was afraid and terrified, while the second man was neither afraid nor terrified; they were led before the king and stood in his presence.
The king said this to them:
"O sirs, what is this quarrel, strife, conflict, and dispute that has arisen between you?
Then those two men rose up and said this to the king: "Listen, Great King; we possess no territory whatsoever on earth."

On a plot of land borrowed for the occasion, a tree was planted; on that very day it was planted, on that very day sprouts, leaves, flowers, and fruits appeared—half raw and half ripe. And by this second man, on that very same day, a tree was planted in that very same plot of ground.
And of that tree, no sprouts grow;
because it was shaken by the wind, neither leaves, nor flowers, nor fruits appeared.
Moreover, O Great King, its root does not go even one yojana beneath the earth.
"This man is disputing with me, claiming it is your fault. However, Your Majesty, you should know by examining the matter yourself; there is no fault whatsoever on my part in this.
Then the king summoned thirty billion ministers and, having gathered them together, spoke thus:
"Tell me, what do you say? The ministers replied, "What shall we say, Great King?
The king said, "Where have you seen or heard of such a thing—that on the very same day a tree is planted, on that very same day its sprout emerges?"
"Leaves, flowers, and fruits grow;
they are half-ripe and half-unripe—this is the certainty that you must establish.

Then those ministers rose from their seats and said this to the king: "Great King, it does not befit us to make this determination, nor shall we be able to state a definitive conclusion on this matter."
"This is a marvel, O Great King! This very man must be questioned. Say, O man, is this matter true that you speak?
He replied, "It is true, O Great King, that this matter is so. The King said:
(64) We have never heard nor indeed believed such difficult-to-accept words of yours:
that on the very day a tree was planted, it sprouted on that same day;
(65) and that on that very same day you say it gave forth leaves, flowers, and fruit.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, that man said to the king:
"Go yourself and sow the seed; see whether a sprout will grow."
Then, indeed, that king went out together with thirty *koṭis* of ministers;
he had those two men imprisoned in a jail,
and thereafter the king himself planted a tree.
Yet that tree gave forth neither sprouts, nor leaves, nor flowers, nor fruits.
Then the king, becoming enraged, spoke thus:
"Go, sirs, and quickly bring axes for felling wood!"
When that man had brought them back, the tree he had planted appeared with leaves, flowers, and fruit; yet out of anger, he cut down that tree.

When that single tree was cut down, twelve trees appeared; when those twelve trees were cut down, twenty-four trees appeared—made of the seven precious gems, complete with roots, leaves, flowers, and sprouts. Then, from those twenty-four...
From the trees, twenty-four birds appeared—
cocks with golden crests and golden beaks, their feathers composed of the seven precious gems.
Then, overcome by rage, the king took an axe in his own hand and struck that tree.
Then, from that tree which has been struck, nectar-water flows forth.
Thereupon, the king, with a deeply moved mind, issues a command.

"Go, and release those two men from their prison bonds. "So be it, Your Majesty," they replied. At that very moment, having run forth, they released those two men from their prison bonds and led them to where that tree was. Then the king asked:
"How is it that this tree, planted by you, being cut down as one, grows back twofold, until it has become twenty-fourfold?"

"The tree planted by me has gone away; it has not produced any sprouts, leaves, flowers, or fruits. Then that man spoke thus: "Great King, such as my merits are, such merits do not exist for you. Then those thirty koṭis of ministers, having placed both their knees upon the ground, spoke thus: "You must exercise the sovereignty; this [man] shall not."
The former king shone with splendor.
Then that man addressed those ministers in verse:
(66cd) I have no need for royal power or enjoyments, nor for grain or wealth;
(67) my aspiration is toward the Buddhas: may I become the supreme among bipeds.
For the Tathāgata would indeed go to the peaceful realm of nirvāṇa,
where he might teach you the Dharma that leads to the city of nirvāṇa.
Then, having assumed the cross-legged posture, he made this vow:
"Whatever evil I previously committed has brought me to this imprisonment by the king;
but by making this aspiration, may my evil be exhausted."
Then indeed, those twenty-four koṭis of birds and cocks struck the musical instruments with their diamond-beaks.
Then, at that time and on that occasion, thirty-two thousand gabled pavilions appeared.
Each individual gabled pavilion manifested with a measurement of twenty-five yojanas, and within each gabled pavilion, twenty-five birds— cocks— appeared,
with golden crests, golden beaks, and golden faces.
They uttered human speech:
"It was not well done by you, O Great King, that this tree was cut down;
for hundreds of millions of trees have stood here once more."
"By this evil deed, you shall experience an undesirable result.
You do not know what kind of being it was by whom this tree was planted.
The king said:
(72) "I do not know this matter; O Great Ascetic, please explain it clearly:
what kind of being is that great being by whom this tree was planted? The birds said: (73) "For he shall arise as a Guide, a light of the world."
He is the liberator of all sentient beings from the bonds of existence within saṃsāra.
The king said:
(74) "Which is the second being whose tree does not grow? Or what evil deed was committed by him? Tell me, O twice-born ones."
The birds said:
"Devadatta is indeed a fool, for the tree does not grow upon him.
Since no merit has been performed by him, how can a tree grow for him?"

Then, at that time and on that occasion, thirty koṭis of ministers, having heard this Dharma discourse, all became Bodhisattvas established in the ten stages (daśabhūmi) and attained the supernormal knowledges (abhijñā); and that king, established in the ten stages, attained the realization of wholesome dharmas (kuśaladharma-abhisamaya).
[SaSū 215] Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition, by which thirty million people have become established on the ten stages and have attained the supernormal powers?
The Blessed One said: "Listen, Bhaiṣajyasena; I shall explain it to you."
Then, at that very moment, the Blessed One manifested a smile.
Immediately upon that occasion, from the Blessed One’s mouth, eighty-four hundred thousand rays of light issued forth— of many colors, various colors, and hundreds of thousands of different colors,
such as blue, yellow, red, white, madder-red, crystal, and silver.
Having illuminated those infinite and boundless world-systems, they returned once more,
circumambulated the Blessed One three times to the right, and vanished into the crown of the Blessed One’s head.
Then, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena rose from his seat and draped his robe over one shoulder.

Having draped his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, he addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the condition for manifesting this smile?
For Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do not manifest a smile without cause or without condition."
The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, do you see the masses of people coming from all directions throughout the world-system to my presence?
He replied: "No indeed, Blessed One, I do not see them."
The Blessed One said: "In that case, Bhaiṣajyasena, look out and behold the multitude of people.

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena, having looked out, saw in the eastern direction a single tree that had appeared, measuring seven thousand yojanas in size; there, on one side, were twenty-five thousand koṭis.
The masses of people had gathered there;

yet they did not speak, nor did they converse, nor address one another, nor engage in conversation; they did not eat, nor did they rise, nor did they walk about, but remained patient in silence. To the south, a single tree appeared, measuring seven thousand yojanas in size, where twenty-five thousand koṭis of the masses of people had gathered.
They do not chatter, they do not converse, they do not talk;
they do not speak, they do not rise, and they do not walk about;
they acquiesce through silence.
In the western direction, a single tree appeared, measuring seven thousand yojanas in size; there, twenty-five thousand koṭis of people gathered.
They did not speak, nor did they converse, nor did they chat; they did not utter words, nor did they stand up, nor did they walk about.
They consent by remaining silent.
In the northern direction, a single tree appeared, measuring seven thousand yojanas in size; there, twenty-five thousand koṭis of people gathered.
They did not speak, nor did they converse, nor did they chat, nor did they utter a word, nor did they stand up.
They did not walk about; they remained in silence, accepting [the situation].
In the upward direction, a single tree appeared, measuring seven thousand yojanas in height; there, twenty-five thousand koṭis of people gathered.
They did not speak, nor did they converse, nor did they chat, nor did they utter a word.
They did not rise, nor did they walk about;
they remained there, accepting it through silence. To the lower direction, a tree appeared, measuring seven thousand yojanas in height, and there a gathering of twenty-five billion people assembled.
They did not speak, they did not converse, they did not talk, they did not address one another, they did not rise, nor did they walk about; they remained patient in silence.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena said this to the Blessed One:
"I would like to ask the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, about a certain matter, if the Blessed One would grant me the opportunity to have my question answered."

When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena: "Ask, Bhaiṣajyasena, whatever you desire; I shall satisfy your mind by answering each and every question you have asked.
When this had been said, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena spoke thus to the Blessed One:

"Lord, why is it that this multitude of people has come and stationed itself throughout the world-systems in the four directions, even as far as fifty *koṭis* of beings have come and stationed themselves from below up to the zenith; and yet they do not address the Blessed One, nor converse with him,
nor speak, nor talk, nor utter a word?"
"They do not rise, nor do they walk about;
they remain silent and endure it.
"Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason? The Blessed One said: "Go, Bhaiṣajyasena, and ask those Tathāgatas yourself."
Since these multitudes of people have come from this world-system,
he asked: "Lord, by whose empowerment of supernatural power do I go?"
"Is it by the power of the Tathāgata’s supernatural might, or by your own?
The Blessed One said, "Go, Bhaiṣajyasena, by the empowerment of your own power of supernatural might;
then return again by the power of the Tathāgata’s supernatural might."

Then indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena, having circumambulated the Blessed One three times, vanished right there. Then, having passed beyond ninety-six *koṭis* of world-systems from this world-system, there is a world-system named Candrapradīpa;
therein dwells at present the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Candrāvatikṣetra.
He remained, was sustained, and continued to live;
surrounded and honored by a retinue of eighty thousand *koṭīs* of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, he was teaching the Dharma.
The bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyasena arrived at that world-system.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena approached the Blessed One;

having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Candrāvatīkṣetra, and standing before him, he extended his joined palms in reverence toward the Blessed One.

He said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, having come from the Sahā world-system, the buddha-field of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, after crossing ninety-six thousand million world-systems, I have not seen so many sentient beings anywhere else, Blessed One."

"World-Honored One, what is the cause and what is the condition that a great multitude of people has gathered before the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Śākyamuni, in this Sahā world-system, having come from the ten directions? While standing right here, I see them as they were there, yet being where I am now, I do not see them."
The Blessed One said: “Bhaiṣajyasena, they move about and dwell right there. He asked:
“But how is it, Blessed One? The Blessed One said: “Sentient beings are produced from insentient trees.”
He asked: "Blessed One, by whom has it been seen, or by whom has it been heard, that humans are born from an insentient tree?
The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, you have not seen [it]," nor have you heard it.
Nor has it been heard that humans are born from an insentient tree.
He said:
“Blessed One, I have neither seen nor heard of humans being born from an insentient tree.
The Blessed One said, “Bhaiṣajyasena, do you wish to see it? I shall show it to you right now. He replied, “I do.”
"I desire it, Blessed One; I desire it, Sugata.
Then, at that moment, the Tathāgata Candrāvatikṣetra extended his own arm, which was variegated by a hundred merits.
And from that arm, hundreds of thousands of millions of groups of people appeared; and each group of people, extending a hundred arms, scattered various perfumes and ointments over the Tathāgata.
Then the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Candrāvatikṣetra, addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena:
"Bhaiṣajyasena, do you see this multitude of people scattering various perfumes, garlands, and ointments over the Tathāgata? He replied: "I see them, Blessed One."
"I see them, Blessed One; I see them, Sugata.
The Blessed One said: "These senseless masses of people have appeared; these senseless men have been reborn."
Then, indeed, the hundred arms of each one of those hundreds of thousands of millions were all severed.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena, having seen this, said this to the Blessed One:
"What is this, Blessed One? What is this, Sugata, that in a mere moment the hundred arms of these men have been severed?"
“Blessed One, if even those with a hundred arms are not liberated, what need is there to mention two-armed humans?
The Blessed One said, “It is just so, Bhaiṣajyasena; insentient beings are born, and insentient beings cease.”
"Bhaiṣajyasena, our own bodies also should be considered as having become insentient.
He asked, "Blessed One, which beings are young, and which are old? The Blessed One said, "Bhaiṣajyasena, there are beings who are young, and there are those who are old. He asked:
“Blessed One, which are the young ones and which are the old?
He replied: “Those that are currently scattered are the old; those that have just emerged from the trees are the young. He asked:
“Blessed One, I wish to see young beings.
Then, that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Candrāvatikṣetra, extended his right palm. Thereupon, hundreds of thousands of millions of groups of people came from the ten directions.
From the direction below, fifty koṭis of beings arrived.

Having arrived, those multitudes of beings bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One; yet they did not address the Tathāgata, nor did they converse with him, but remained silent and showed their assent.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, why is it that these beings do not address the Tathāgata, nor do they converse with him?"
They consent by remaining silent.
The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, do you not know that this spot of earth is insentient? It does not speak, nor does it converse; it does not discern the mass of Dharma."
For what reason? Bhaiṣajyasena, there are some young beings here who do not know arising and do not know cessation.

Even upon seeing [these things], they do not perceive old age, sickness, sorrow, lamentation, separation from the beloved, union with the unloved, being deprived of the beloved, death, or untimely death;
nor, having seen all those bitter sufferings, do they apply themselves with effort—how then shall they come to know [them]?
"Bhaiṣajyasena, you must instruct them again and again.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, from where do these young beings come? From where do they pass away?"
"Where are those reborn who do not know (or understand) the Dharma?
The Blessed One said, "Listen, Bhaiṣajyasena, as to what kind of human body they take on."
That was not made by a silversmith,
nor was it made by a leatherworker,
nor was it made by a carpenter.
It is not made by a potter;
it does not arise out of fear of a king.
Through the union of male and female, that which is joined with evil karma comes into being.
Again and again, they teach those beings various crafts;
yet for them, an endless and bitter suffering arises.
There, they experience the ripening of the evil karmas previously committed, which are bitter sensations.
Bhaiṣajyasena, it is right here that these young beings have come who do not speak, do not converse, and do not rise— those who experience such painful sensations.
For this reason, Bhaiṣajyasena, they do not speak and do not converse.
In this way, Bhaiṣajyasena, those young beings, being ignorant of what is wholesome, do not know arising and do not know cessation;
nor will they obtain a human existence.
These, Bhaiṣajyasena, are called "young beings."
He asked: "Blessed One, how do young beings arise, and how do they cease?
The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, it is just as if some man were to rub wood with wood to produce fire; gradually that wood would be set ablaze by the fire.
In the very same way, Bhaiṣajyasena, the human body first comes into being."
And once born, he experiences sensation.
He asked: "Who here is born by noble birth? Who has entered final nirvāṇa? The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, only a Buddha is born by noble birth; only a Tathāgata has entered final nirvāṇa."

Bhaiṣajyasena, it is just as if, for example, a king were to have a man imprisoned and confined within a certain dark house, a chamber of gloom. That man, having entered the dark house, would see the interior of the house as a place of darkness and gloom. Then, another man, seeing him, might think of him due to his previous experiences of suffering and consider him lost.
This man, unaccustomed to hardship, will meet his destruction while still alive.

He would bring fire there and cast a small spark of fire inside that inner room; and that man, confined within the prison, would see the flame of that fire, and upon seeing it, he would become comforted and increase his resolve; and that fire, for some reason or other, would burst into a blaze.

And by that blazing fire, that house would be set ablaze on all sides, and that man would be burned right there. When the king heard that he had been burned, he would fall into anxiety and distress. It would occur to him: "I shall no longer place any sentient being under confinement in a prison within my own realm.
Then that king would thus reassure those beings dwelling in his realm: "Do not be afraid, sirs; do not tremble!"

May you have no fear; henceforth, within my realm, there shall be no further infliction of punishment nor imprisonment for anyone. Furthermore, I shall not cause the destruction of the life of any living being.
"Be fearless, O beings; may you become so.

In this very way, Bhaiṣajyasena, the Tathāgata has burned away all afflictions and pacified all diseases, just as that man burned his own body from the house fire—for the sake, welfare, and happiness of all sentient beings."
He has set out [on this path];

he would liberate beings from slaughter, bondage, and imprisonment. In exactly the same way, the Tathāgata—having abandoned the stains of passion, hatred, and delusion—has arisen as a lamp for the world and liberates beings from the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, and asuras.
He liberates both young beings and old beings.
Then, at that very moment, these verses issued forth from the sky above:
(76) Oh, what a field! The field of the Victors is a well-prepared, excellent field, wherein seeds once sown never come to destruction.
(77) The Buddha-field is the field of the Victors; the teaching of the Victors is most praiseworthy.
The Teacher indeed employs skillful means for the sake of gathering all sentient beings;
though established in the realm of nirvāṇa, he appears upon the surface of the earth.
Having brought peace to the entire world, the Buddha purifies the sacrificial offerings.
(79) He liberates new beings and he liberates those who are ancient;
having liberated all beings from the triple world in due order,
(80) the gates of hell are indeed closed, and the animals and hungry ghosts are set free.
For peace has been established in this world, and happiness has been secured in the next world.
[SaSū 232] Then, at that time, the Blessed One manifested a smile and said:
(81) "Excellent is the sight of the virtuous Buddhas; excellent is the sight of them. Excellent is the field of the qualities of the Dharma; excellent is the sight of the harmony of the Saṃgha."
(82) "Excellent! Those who hear this sutra, this instruction on the *Saṃghāṭa* which destroys all evil, shall attain the unsurpassed state.
Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena, having extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason..."
This was the reason for manifesting a smile.
The Blessed One said, "Son of good family, do you see these young beings? He replied, "I see them."
"I see them, Blessed One; I see them, Sugata.
The Blessed One said: "Bhaiṣajyasena, all these will this very day become bodhisattvas established on the ten stages."
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena stood eighty thousand *yojanas* above in the sky;
then eighty thousand *koṭis* of sons of gods rained down a rain of flowers over the Blessed One, and those young beings, having seen this, all joined their palms in reverence and paid homage.
Then, indeed, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena, while remaining in mid-air, uttered these words,
which filled the trichiliocosm with sound;
the beings reborn in the thirty-two great hells heard that sound.
The thirty-two classes of gods heard that sound;
the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system shook in six ways; eighty-four thousand dragon kings were agitated within the great ocean;
and thirty trillion *rākṣasa*s came to this Jambūdvīpa.
Twenty-five thousand koṭis of pretas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas arrived at the royal capital of Aḍakavatī, and a great assembly was established before the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One taught the Dharma to those young beings.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas from hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of world-systems in the ten directions arrived by means of their respective supernatural powers.
Then the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena, having extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One, said:
He said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, Sugata, many bodhisattvas have gathered and are seated;
and many gods and nāgas, Blessed One, have also gathered and are seated.
Furthermore, numerous rākṣasas and pretas, having come to the capital city of Aḍakavatī, have gathered and are seated to hear the Dharma."
[SaSū 237] Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena: "Come, son of good family!

Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena, descending from above by means of his supernatural power, joined his palms toward where the Blessed One was and said this to the Blessed One: "The aggregate of Dharma..."
"Regarding the term 'aggregate of Dharma' (dharmaskandha):
Blessed One, by how much is it said that something is called an 'aggregate of Dharma'?
The Blessed One replied: 'Noble son, regarding the term "aggregate of Dharma," it is said as follows.'"
"Whoever seeks the holy life, having sought the holy life, desists from all evil.
Do you see, noble son, these young beings who desist from unchastity?
He replied, "I see them, Blessed One; I see them, Sugata. The Buddha said:
They will surely have attained the dhāraṇīs and will be endowed with all dharmas. He said:
"By what means, Blessed One, have so many beings gathered here to hear the aggregate of the Dharma? Then the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Bhaiṣajyasena:
Bhaiṣajyasena, there are many beings who do not even hear that birth itself is suffering,
and who do not even hear that old age itself is suffering.

They do not hear that illness itself is suffering; nor do they hear that the suffering of grief, the suffering of lamentation, the suffering of separation from the beloved, and the suffering of association with the unloved exist. But death carries away all suffering.
Bhaiṣajyasena, this body and life are said to be all suffering.
[SaSū 239] Then those young beings, having heard this teaching, extended their joined palms toward where the Blessed One was and said this to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, must we too die?
The Blessed One said: "Noble sons, you too, as well as all sentient beings, must die."
He asked: "Blessed One, how does the time of death arrive?

The Blessed One replied: "At the time of death, noble son, within the final consciousness, there arises the wind called 'cessation of consciousness' (*vijñānanirodha*), which is a delusion of consciousness."

The wind called "name," and the wind associated with the agitation of consciousness— these three winds, O son of good family, at the time of death, churn the final consciousness, cause it to be disturbed,
and produce agitation within it.
They said:
"Blessed One, what are those three that strike down the body when consciousness is ceasing at the time of death? The Blessed One said: "O friends, they are called Śastraka, Sūcaka, and Ṣṭhīlaka."
Those who destroy the body.
He asked: "Blessed One, what is this that is called 'body'?"
The Blessed One said: "O worthy ones, there is one called Ādīptaka, one called Dahanavāsaka, one called Meḍika, and one called Śṛṅgārika."
One who is called "a dweller in cemeteries," one who is called "of poor intellect," and one who is called "burdened by heavy loads."
It is called "afflicted by birth," it is called "agitated by birth," and it is called "that which exhausts life."
And there is that which is called death and separation from the beloved;
these, friends, are called by the name of the body.
They asked: "Blessed One, how does one die? How does one live?"
The Blessed One said: "Venerable ones, it is consciousness that dies; venerable ones, it is merit that lives.
Friends, it is the body that dies—it is bound by millions of sinews, bound by eighty-four thousand veins and arteries, and bound by twelve thousand members."
The body is bound together by three hundred and sixty bones; within it dwell eighty-four thousand families of worms, and the death of all those living beings occurs there.
There is also the cessation of their death; when that happens, all those creatures become hopeless.
When that person dies, then a turbulent agitation of the wind-stuff arises among all those living beings for the sake of devouring one another, and at that time they experience painful sensations.
Others, however, grieve for their sons;
others grieve for their daughters or their kinsmen. Pierced by the arrows of grief, they all begin to devour one another.
Thus, they all gradually devour each other in succession.
Two living beings remain;
they fight for seven days, and when the seven days have passed, one living being is crushed and the other is released.
Venerable ones, what is called "the Dharma"? What do you think? Just as all living beings die through mutual destruction, even so do foolish common people fall into mutual conflict;
yet they do not fear birth.
They do not fear diseases;
they do not fear death.
Just as those two living beings were fighting, even so do foolish ordinary people fight with one another.
Then, at the time of death, he is addressed by good men: "O man, why do you place such trust [in this world]?
Have you not seen any misfortune in the human realm? Have you not seen the misfortune of birth, nor the misfortune of old age, nor the misfortune of illness?"
"The danger of death has not been seen.

He replied, "Venerable sirs, the danger of birth has been seen by me; the danger of old age and the danger of sickness have been seen; and finally, the danger of death has been seen. He [the interlocutor] said:

Why have you not performed those roots of merit which ought to be performed? O man, why have you not cultivated the roots of merit consisting of the aggregates of Dharma, which bring about welfare in both worlds?
Friends, I ask you a second time.

"Why have you not accumulated the equipment of roots of merit, by which you might be liberated from birth, old age, sickness, and death? Why have you not practiced the examination through wise attention?
Have you, O man, heard the sound of the gong being struck upon the earth?"

Furthermore, you have not seen the humans of Jambudvīpa giving gifts, performing meritorious deeds, observing fasts, or planting seeds of roots of virtue in the field of the Tathāgata; nor have you seen them offering incense, garlands, or lamps, nor food and drink being given; nor have you seen the four assemblies of the Tathāgata.
Being thus gratified, whether they be a monk, a nun, a layman, or a laywoman—these four assemblies who are firmly established in the teaching—they speak and converse with him for his benefit, saying:
"O man, nothing at all has been done by the gods that is unfavorable; rather, it is you who have accomplished this by coming to this Jambudvīpa."
[SaSū 242] When that person has died, at that time Dharmarāja, instructing him, speaks these verses:
"Having seen the appearance of a Tathāgata, having heard the striking of the gaṇḍī,
and having heard the teaching of the Dharma which is peaceful and leads to Nirvāṇa..."
(84) "Why did you not perform merit that brings happiness in the next world?
You shall experience suffering in hell, the fruit of undesirable karma.
Then that man replied to the King of Dharma with verses:
(85) I was of childish intellect, following the influence of evil friends; I committed sinful deeds with a mind deluded by desire.
(86) And because of my desire for that [object], its terrible fruit has arrived:
I have committed violence against living beings and destroyed the property of the Saṅgha. (87) With a corrupted and evil mind, I have even caused the destruction of a stūpa.
Harsh speech was uttered: "My mother has been tormented."
(88) I recognize the transgression committed by my own body; I see my rebirth in the most dreadful Raurava hell. (89) I shall experience suffering in Saṃghāta and likewise in Pratāpana.
And in the Mahāvīci hell, I shall experience bitter sensations; and in the Mahāpadma hell, I shall cry out, deeply afflicted by suffering;
and a hundred times I shall be born in the Kālasūtra hell, which is full of great terror.
(91) And even when the hell-beings have been struck down, they again behold that terror;
they encounter once more a great fear extending for a hundred yojanas.
(92) Being tormented again in the cauldron, they will not find an exit.
There is a hell named Kṣūra, consisting of a thousand razor-edged blades;
before it, hundreds of thousands of millions of razors arise.
By means of those, his body is split apart due to his own evil deeds.
